Shadow Tactics is Commandos with ninjas. That’s a good thing, by the way. Very few games swim in the same genre pool as Shadow Tactics. There was the Commandos series, and the Desperados games, and that’s basically it. So all Shadow Tactics has to do is take the “shepherd 2-5 killers during their sneak-and-murder spree across a bunch of maps” to Edo period Japan to feel fresh and original. This means that there is only one question to ask if you want to know if Shadow Tactics is worth your time: Would you like to play more Commandos, or Desperados? For me the answer was “It’s complicated”. I played Commandos way back when. I liked the gameplay at first: Sneaking across the map littered with guards until you find the one unfortunate soul not covered by his colleagues and murder the bejeesus out of him, then moving on the guy whose back he was watching, and so on, pulling on the thread of the guard sweater until only a frayed collar remains… It’s like a beautiful puzzle that drips blood for every piece you set down. But the difficulty spikes were brutal, and at times the precision and speed with which a kill was only possible took so many tries for me to get right that I got frustrated and finally gave up on Commandos. These frustrating moments and difficulty spikes are in here, too, but Shadow Tactics does just enough to mitigate the frustrations that I stuck it out. The excellent quicksave system is one factor: not only does it remind you how long it’s been since your last save, it automatically rotates three slots so that when you save in a situation you don’t yet know is beyond saving, you can revert to an earlier save. The adding of banter between the characters is helpful, too. The story might be kind of rote and have a giant plot hole at the center of it, but the characters are well fleshed out, for the genre, and the dialogue script as well as the voice work elevate the game quite a bit. And yes, it helps that I sneak around ancient japanese fortresses and abduct the son **** from a Sento instead of traipsing around european battefields and assassinating **** commanders, again. Success in Shadow Tactics relies on split second timing at times. That can only work if the controls of the game are excellent, and luckily, they are: Switching between characters and ordering them to do stuff is effortless. The art is serviceable to good: Clearly legible, beautiful at times, but lacking any true wow moments. The sound is sparse but well done, the music unobtrusive and pleasing. The voice work is, as mentioned, well above average for this type of game. This game is for veterans of the genre with a taste for more, spiced with a bit of variation. Complete newcomers interested in the genre might as well start here: They might still bounce off Shadow Tactics, but in a genre with very few members, this is as forgiving as it gets. TLDR: Shadow Tactics is a great stealth real time tactics game. If that’s your jam, it has you covered.

Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun - A Stealthy Symphony in Feudal Japan
Step into the vibrant yet perilous world of 17th-century Japan with Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun. This tactical stealth masterpiece, crafted by Mimimi Games, throws you headfirst into the shoes of six unique ronin and kunoichi, each with their own skills and personalities, tasked with eliminating powerful enemies and navigating intricate levels amidst a backdrop of political intrigue and personal vendettas.

A Shadowy Ballet:

Shadow Tactics' brilliance lies in its meticulous blend of strategy and stealth. Every level unfolds like a meticulously choreographed dance, demanding calculated planning and precise execution. You'll spend hours studying enemy patrol patterns, strategically positioning your characters, and chaining their abilities together to overcome seemingly insurmountable odds.

A Gallery of Lethal Artists:

Your six operatives are more than just pixelated pawns; they're living, breathing individuals with distinct strengths and weaknesses. Hayato, the agile ninja, scales walls and eliminates lone guards with ease. Yuki, the cunning kunoichi, distracts enemies and lays deadly traps. Mugen, the hulking samurai, slices through foes in a whirlwind of steel. Each character demands careful consideration, and mastering their synergy is key to success.

A Feast for the Senses:

Shadow Tactics is a visual and auditory treat. The hand-drawn art style is breathtaking, with lush landscapes, detailed environments, and expressive character animations. The soundtrack is equally captivating, blending traditional Japanese instruments with haunting melodies and heart-pounding action cues. Every element immerses you deeper into the world, heightening the tension and the thrill of each successful maneuver.

A Glimmer in the Darkness:

Despite its unforgiving gameplay and punishing difficulty, Shadow Tactics never feels unfair. Each challenge, no matter how daunting, feels meticulously crafted, offering multiple solutions and rewarding experimentation. The satisfaction of pulling off a flawlessly executed plan, perfectly synchronizing your characters' abilities to eliminate an entire patrol without raising an alarm, is unparalleled.

Not Without Scars:

However, Shadow Tactics isn't without its blemishes. The camera controls can be clunky at times, and the occasional technical hiccup can disrupt the flow of gameplay. The story, while engaging, takes a backseat to the stellar mechanics, and the ending might leave some players wanting more.

A Must-Play for Stealth Aficionados:

Despite these minor flaws, Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun remains a masterclass in the stealth genre. Its innovative gameplay, breathtaking visuals, and unforgettable characters make it a must-play for any fan of strategic thinking and nail-biting tension. So, don your ninja garb, sharpen your katana, and prepare to enter the shadows – Shadow Tactics awaits.

Verdict:

Pros:
Innovative and rewarding tactical stealth gameplay
Diverse and well-developed characters with unique abilities
Stunning hand-drawn art style and immersive soundtrack
Satisfyingly challenging without feeling unfair
Cons:
Clunky camera controls and occasional technical issues
Story takes a backseat to the gameplay
Abrupt ending might leave some players wanting more
Score: 4.5 out of 5 shurikens. A near-flawless stealth masterpiece that will captivate and challenge you in equal measure.

Recommended for: Fans of tactical games, stealth enthusiasts, and lovers of beautiful art and captivating soundtracks.

Not recommended for: Players who prefer action-packed gameplay or dislike challenging difficulty levels.

I hope this review gives you a glimpse into the captivating world of Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun. Whether you're a seasoned shinobi or a curious newcomer, this game is sure to leave you speechless. So, prepare to unleash your inner shadow warrior and dive into this unforgettable experience.

Reviewing (mostly) every game (or DLC) in my library, part 66:

⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️☆ (9/10 stars)

[i] Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun [/i] is a phenomenal real-time tactics game that blends stealth, action, puzzle-solving, and strategy into a tight, beautifully crafted package. Set in Edo-period Japan, it’s as much about patience and planning as it is about precise execution. Every mission feels like a handcrafted stealth puzzle box: one where you slowly, methodically dismantle overwhelming odds with skill and precision. If you’ve ever enjoyed games like [i] Commandos [/i] or [i] Desperados, [/i] this is a spiritual successor done right. If you haven’t? This might just convert you.

🏹 [b] Pros: [/b]
[list]
[*] A stealth masterpiece. Missions are long, intricate, and deeply satisfying. You’re almost always outnumbered, which means success comes from careful observation, timing, and synchronization. It’s a masterclass in stealth design: every kill, distraction, and escape feels earned.

[*] Tight character design. You control a squad of five unique characters, each with their own specialized skill set. From Hayato the nimble ninja, to Yuki the deadly trap-laying thief, to Mugen the samurai tank, all feel distinct and useful in different scenarios. Learning to combine their abilities is half the fun.

[*] Stunning visuals and art direction. The isometric maps are gorgeously detailed, full of living villages, snowy mountains, and moonlit castles. There’s great environmental storytelling baked into each level, with guards chatting, civilians going about their routines, and clever opportunities hidden in plain sight.

[*] Excellent UI and tools. Shadow Mode lets you queue up synchronized actions between characters, allowing for beautifully orchestrated takedowns. The ability to quick save and quick load with a single button makes experimenting stress-free and encourages creative problem-solving.

[*] Smart difficulty design. The game is hard but fair. You’re always told what enemies can see, and success comes from reading and manipulating their patterns. No tricks here.

[*] Cultural immersion. The Japanese voice acting is incredible and adds a lot to the atmosphere. Combined with the historical setting, respectful tone, and visual style, it’s easy to get fully immersed in this world.

[*] Bonus challenges and replayability. Every level comes with optional challenges—like never killing anyone, or finishing under a certain time limit—which encourages replays and mastery without ever feeling forced.
[/list]

⚔️[b] Cons: [/b]
[list]
[*] Can be overwhelming. The game throws you into large, complex maps with lots of moving parts. For new players, it can be intimidating to figure out where to begin or how to approach situations.

[*] Trial-and-error heavy. Some solutions only become clear after multiple failed attempts. If you’re not into the “fail-fast, reload faster” rhythm, this might frustrate you.

[*] Pacing can drag. Because levels are long (some can take over an hour), and you’re encouraged to move slowly and cautiously, the game can feel exhausting in long sessions. It’s best played in focused chunks.

[*] Minor control jank. On controller or handheld (like Steam Deck), precise movement and camera control can be a bit fiddly. Mouse + keyboard remains the ideal setup.
[/list]

Review: Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐

Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun is a brilliant example of how a game can focus on one core idea and execute it to perfection. It’s a strategy masterpiece that rewards patience, planning, and precision. Every level is a puzzle waiting to be solved, and every character you command feels essential to the bigger picture.

Pros:

Deep Strategy Gameplay: Every mission demands clever thinking, timing, and coordination. It’s the kind of game that makes you feel smart when your plan works.

Beautiful Graphics & Design: The art style captures feudal Japan in stunning detail, with vibrant environments that are both gorgeous and functional.

Variety in Levels: Each stage feels different and forces you to adapt your strategy—no two missions play the same.

Interesting Characters: Every character has unique abilities, and the synergy between them adds endless tactical depth.

For Strategy Lovers: If you enjoy games that focus on precision and problem-solving, this is pure genius in its own right.

Polished & Refined: Everything feels carefully designed, from the UI to the level layouts, giving the game a sense of quality rarely seen in its niche.

Cons:

High Difficulty: This isn’t a casual game—mistakes are punished, and trial-and-error is part of the experience.

Niche Appeal: Players looking for fast action might find the methodical pace too slow.

Final Thoughts

Shadow Tactics is a shining gem in the strategy genre. It doesn’t try to be everything—it picks a lane and masters it. For fans of stealth tactics and smart problem-solving, this is one of the best experiences you can play.

In a world full of games that try to do too much, Shadow Tactics reminds us that sometimes less is more—and when done right, it’s genius.

[b]Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun[/b] is one of those rare games that rewards patience, precision, and creative thinking in equal measure. Set in beautifully recreated Edo-period Japan, it plays like a love letter to classic real-time tactics games like Commandos, but with a flair all its own. Every mission feels like an intricately crafted puzzle, and solving it using a team of unique characters—each with their own abilities and personalities—never stops being satisfying.

What really stands out is how human the characters feel. From Mugen’s samurai honor to Yuki’s childlike curiosity and deadly traps, you actually grow attached to them, making every risky move feel personal. The voice acting, especially in Japanese, adds authenticity, and the hand-painted environments are just stunning.

It’s tough, though. Really tough. If you're not into trial-and-error or methodical planning, it might frustrate you. But if you like outsmarting enemies with clever tactics and orchestrating silent takedowns like clockwork, this game is a hidden gem.

Also I would say Shadow Tactics has a better overall story and more enjoyable character development. The entire roster is likable and I cared for the characters. [h1] My strategy was brilliant and my execution brilliantly flawed... [/h1]

This is impressively well crafted tactics games as all games from Mimimi games but this one with a flavor of Edo period Japan. With a well thought out plan and buckets of patience you will master 5  agents of shogunate and fight the uprising against imperial rule.

[h2] It's all about puzzles [/h2]

During various campaign missions you will be put into control of 5 characters with unique ability kits. Each mission is essentially treated as a big puzzle but with multiple solutions. At the start you will scout the maps for available routes, hiding spots and tools to help you solve it. You will learn guards' behavior which will open up new paths or give you hints how, when and in what order you eliminate undesirable enemies along the way. Each mission has a specific characters locked in so you cannot choose your team but in that way all missions are built to really utilize the abilities of these characters to full extent.

[h2] Map design is the king. [/h2]

It is indeed the main pillar that makes this game great. The maps are huge with a lot of interesting areas with plentiful options for your agents to work with. And each and every map does its best to feel natural with seemingly no weaknesses until you start looking at them closely. You will notice hidden paths, weak links in enemy routes or interactive objects that could help to disguise your approach or get rid of enemies without raising any significant suspicion. This pairs nicely with your characters’ abilities and makes you consider which sort of approach you are going to take.

[h2] You make the best with what you have. [/h2]

Do you fancy a ninja that strikes from shadows and the rooftops or rather direct approach in the form of samurai capable of disposing of strong enemies or even groups of weaker enemies. How about a seemingly weak girl who can set up deadly traps, or an old 1-legged man with a very deadly rifle. Perhaps a very attractive woman with a knack for disguise. All of these characters have a mix of melee and range options with various advantages and disadvantages. They also possess other utilities to weaken enemies, lure them, distract them. It is only up to you how you use them.

[h2] Oh shogun, my master... [/h2]

The story is rather simple with predictable events but it sits well with how the game is built and played. Characters are likable enough and missions are varied and well thought out. You will conduct your operations in the cities with luxurious residences and busy streets. In wilderness, on the mountain top temples and in the peasant villages. Anywhere your shogun needs you. And all in modest yet beautiful aesthetics and music that adds so much flavor.

[h1] In conclusion: [/h1]

Shadow Tactics is an excellent stealth strategy game, but it's encumbered by an incredibly frustrating difficulty curve.

At the time I write this, only 19% of players have unlocked the story achievement for completing half the game. Noteably, this is also around the time I stopped having fun.

I'm bringing attention to this achievement to make a point when you compare it to the overall rating the game received. It's a [i]good[/i] game: the story is a little superficial but solid, the characters are unique and interesting, the maps are well designed and lend to creative strategy, and the mechanics feel sturdy.

However, it gets [b]unforgivably f'ing difficult[/b], and the percentage leads me to believe most people quit for this reason.

I played this game on Normal difficulty (Beginner, Hardcore being the alternatives). The number of times I felt the urge to throw my Steam Deck at a wall while playing is probably well into the hundreds.

To quote Mike Tyson, "Everyone has a plan until they get punched in the face." You're going to get punched in the face, a lot. The first dozen times you reform a strategy to clear out the same clutch of enemies and it fails, you think, "Ah man, okay, I think I see what I need to try next time."

So you reload, and suddenly an enemy half way across the map you didn't notice turns at exactly the right moment to catch you picking up a body. So you reload, and an enemy catches your ally on a roof because you forgot to crouch while using another character. So you reload, and a patrolling enemy just happens to catch the slightest glimpse of a body you didn't get to hide. So you reload, and on, and on, and on.

Around the 10th level (of 13 in total), I decided to switch to Beginner difficulty just so I could enjoy the remainder of the game. Frankly, I don't really see much of a difference.

One of the achievements requires you to finish the game in Hardcore mode while collecting all the badges (challenges) unique to each map. This includes performing special kills, completion under a specific time, avoiding certain terrain, etc.

This achievement has a 1.4% completion rate, because you [i]have to be filled with masochistic self-loathing[/I] to find this achievement enjoyable. As an achievement hunter, this will be the only achievement I won't even bother attempting.

In summary:
[list]
[*] Is Shadow Tactics good: yes.
[*] Do I recommend playing it: yes.
[*] Is it going to make you angry: yes.
[/list]
Based on the midpoint achievement, you stand roughly an 80% chance of rage-quitting the game before you reach the middle. Given that there are a number of reasons someone might stop a game early, let's be generous and call it 50%.

So, make of that what you will.

This isn’t some frenzied, top-down action game; Shadow Tactics is strategic, methodical, and refreshingly hardcore. One of the best tactical strategy games i ve played. You’ve got hints of Metal Gear Solid and Hitman in there, infused with a bit of Tenchu and more than a little of the venerable Commandos series.

If you haven’t guessed already, the game takes place during Japan’s Edo period, a time of samurai, ninjas, and epic clan wars. Despite achieving unification and years of peace, the shogun senses a looming threat, enlisting an unlikely team of misfits and burdening them with the fate of Japan.

Led by the honour-bound Mugen, Shadow Tactics has you controlling a warrior, spy, shinobi, thief, and sharpshooter as they infiltrate and assassinate using a medley of unique skills. As the player, you will control them one at a time, sneaking past patrols, taking out targets, and completing a variety of objectives.

This is all done in real time, albeit from a top-down perspective, and although Shadow Tactics can be likened to other stealth action games, it comes out as something rather unique.

The game is at its best when combining character abilities to lure, distract, and take down guards without being seen. It can definitely feel a bit trial and error at times though this does little to diminish that sense of reward when a plan is executed perfectly. Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun, developed by Mimimi Games and released on Steam in 2016, is a masterclass in stealth tactics that revitalizes a genre many had written off as dormant. Channeling the spirit of classics like Commandos and Desperados, this game blends old-school real-time strategy mechanics with modern design sensibilities and a unique Edo-period Japanese setting. What emerges is an experience that is both demanding and rewarding, a thinking player’s game where every move must be deliberate, and every mistake is an opportunity to learn.

Set in the early Edo period, Shadow Tactics places players in control of a team of five uniquely skilled characters, each offering a distinct tactical utility. The story follows a ragtag group of operatives—led by the stoic samurai Hayato—who are tasked with rooting out a shadowy conspiracy threatening the Shogunate. Joining Hayato are characters like the cunning ninja Yuki, the deceptive and alluring Aiko, the mighty samurai Mugen, and the mysterious marksman Takuma with his loyal pet tanuki. Each mission unfurls against the backdrop of beautiful hand-crafted environments, from snowy fortresses to coastal towns and ancient temples, with a level of care in visual detail that complements the precision of the gameplay.

The core gameplay loop is pure tactical stealth. Missions are large, open-ended playgrounds with multiple infiltration routes, enemy patrols, traps, and environmental hazards. Players must scout the terrain, study guard movements, and execute synchronized actions using the “Shadow Mode” mechanic, which allows simultaneous commands to be issued to multiple characters. There are no overpowered tools or brute force solutions here—combat is rarely viable, and detection usually leads to swift death. Instead, players are encouraged to use observation and timing to create windows of opportunity: distract one guard with a whistle, lure another with a sake bottle, and quietly take down a third when no one is watching. The satisfaction comes from the chain of perfectly executed moves leading to the seamless elimination of threats.

Each character’s toolkit reinforces the need for coordination and forethought. Hayato is a classic ninja—capable of silent kills and throwing shuriken—but he lacks the raw strength of Mugen, who can carry bodies and dispatch multiple enemies in a single sweep. Yuki’s traps and agility make her ideal for luring and isolating targets, while Aiko can disguise herself and sow confusion from within enemy ranks. Takuma’s sniper rifle has devastating range but limited ammunition, and his frailty makes him best kept at a distance. Success in Shadow Tactics isn’t just about mastering individual characters; it’s about understanding how they complement one another and using them in harmony.

The game’s challenge is formidable, but it is rarely unfair. Every guard, line of sight, and patrol route is clearly communicated, and the quick-save/quick-load system allows for rapid iteration. The game encourages experimentation and rewards creative thinking, but it demands patience and planning. There is immense joy in finding your own path through a heavily guarded area and executing it flawlessly, especially when your plan involves clever use of the terrain—such as dropping a boulder, cutting a rope bridge, or using noise to create a distraction. Few modern games offer this kind of cerebral, rewarding tension.

Visually, Shadow Tactics uses an isometric perspective with painterly detail that brings feudal Japan to life. The environments are vibrant and filled with subtle touches that add to immersion—villagers go about their business, guards chatter, and the weather changes the mood of a level. Characters are stylized but expressive, and the animations are smooth enough to give every action a tangible sense of weight and consequence. The game also features a strong Japanese voice cast that adds authenticity, although the English dub is serviceable for those who prefer it.

Narratively, the game is stronger than one might expect for a tactics-focused title. While the story of political intrigue and rebellion isn’t groundbreaking, it is well-executed, with thoughtful character development and dialogue that highlights each member’s personality. The dynamics between the team members evolve throughout the campaign, especially as secrets come to light and personal motivations clash with duty. These interactions give emotional stakes to what could otherwise be a purely mechanical experience. The final missions in particular have real emotional weight, driven by the characters’ arcs and the culmination of everything you've learned.

Beyond the main campaign, Shadow Tactics offers a high level of replayability. Optional badges challenge players to complete missions in specific ways—such as avoiding kills or never using certain abilities—encouraging experimentation and mastery. The level design supports this flexibility, offering multiple solutions to every problem. For those who crave additional challenge, higher difficulties crank up enemy awareness and reduce margins for error, making success feel even more hard-won.

Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun is a rare gem—an expertly crafted tactical stealth game that respects the player’s intelligence and rewards methodical thinking. It stands out not only for its mechanical precision and elegant design but also for its dedication to atmosphere, character, and cultural authenticity. It’s a love letter to a forgotten genre, modernized just enough to feel fresh without sacrificing the depth that made those earlier games great. Whether you’re a veteran of Commandos or a newcomer to the world of real-time tactics, Shadow Tactics is a brilliant, deeply satisfying experience that demands and deserves your full attention.

[b][i]Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun[/i][/b] is a tactical stealth game in the Edo period setting (Japan). There are no RPG elements in story or gameplay - the characters' personalities and abilities are set in stone (except the early-acquired guns). The story follows a team of spies and assassins working for the local lord. 

The game is very well made - the team is diverse, from a teen hunter to a samurai, the levels are challenging (there are numerous optional challenges and difficulty settings), the controls are rebindable, saving is possible at any time. The graphics and visual design are gorgeous, the voice acting (English) and soundtrack are fitting. Additionally, the characters comment on the actions or events, though it does not change the general story (e.g. whether all hostiles were killed or not). 

In terms of audio and visual accessibility, there are settings for highlighting interactive objects and NPCs and enabling subtitles. The only drawbacks are the lack of the pause function, the inability to order the characters to run when executing the Shadow Mode commands, and the Mimimi logo. The latter is possible to solve by removing the video file.

I’ve had this game in my library for a long time, and while I did love what I tried of it at the time, I never really quite got around to really playing it.  That was, until recently, and man was I missing out.  Shadow Tactics is a RTT stealth game that centers around a party of five unique characters, hired by the shogun to investigate the chaos forming in Edo Japan.

The cast is well-designed, making them unique both in-game and as characters, and the challenges presented will require all of their talents.  The overarching plot is fine, but it’s really the moment to moment gameplay and character-driven narratives that make it worth remembering.  The settings, setpieces, and music are also great and immersive.

I’ve always treated stealth games as a really big puzzle, breaking things down step by step to get to the end goal.  With such a varied cast, there are many ways to approach problems, supported by the variety of objectives presented within the game.  I definitely have opinions on what the “easiest” way to approach a level was, but I know what I did was just one of many.  The quicksave/load system also encourages that experimentation, making trial and error quick and painless.  It really is fundamentally strong overall.

At the time I bought it, I really didn’t know what I was missing out on.  It’s clear to me now that Mimimi Games is the king of RTT stealth, and now I’m hooked.  They really understood what made the genre good and put their own original spin on it.  They’ve got some new games coming out too, and I’m excited to see how things go!

I really enjoy this game. The setting, the story, the characters, all of it is great. The game-play especially is a lot of fun. However, it may not be what you are expecting, especially from the trailers. The way I like to look at it and think about it, is that it is a very elaborate puzzle game. It is just that the pieces are all moving around.

If you want to beat this game, you will need to really use and comprehend all of the different abilities that each of the different characters can use, how you can synergize them, and importantly, synchronize them. Timing is extremely important in this game, it is why I like to look at it like a very detailed puzzle game. Specific guards looking in different directions at certain times, patrol routines, civilian pathing throughout the levels. These are all things that you need to look at, examine, and time all of your actions perfectly in order to get through.

While it may look like you can play it like a fast action kind of game, and there is a sort of time trial mode for each level, a lot of your time playing will be figuring out just the right combination of actions, and when to use them, in order to make your way through one obstacle, to the next, and then onto your objective. If I sound like I am complaining, that is not my intention. I really love this system and the game.

The music is always fantastic, and having different sound effects added into the mix when you use different abilities/take down enemies is really really wonderful. The game is absolutely gorgeous in terms of looks and level design. Never in my time playing the game did I think that I wasn't in Edo Japan. I also really did like the English voice acting and the different characters. I don't think I would like the game half as much if it wasn't for their conversations while you play the game and in cut-scenes. The only thing that kind of threw me off is when some, very few, characters don't do a Japanese accent (*cough* Yuki *cough*), while the vast majority do. I don't understand why this is.

Regardless, I would really, really recommend this game. There can be times where it is a little frustrating, but as soon as you figure it out and get that 'aha!' moment and essentially solve the "puzzle" that has been thwarting you, it is a really great feeling. However, I would recommend that you get the game on sale. The fact that it has been out for seven years and it is still at $50, is a little bit much.

Each mission map is well designed, with lots of colour and detail, beaches, lakes, bustling towns, mansions, castles, and more, all in traditional Japanese style. There are multiple paths you can take through each map, on the ground, using bushes and other objects for cover, using wagons and other vehicles to bypass sections of the map, secret passages, or across the rooftops. The difficulty gradually ramps up with each mission, there’s plenty of “accident” kill opportunities and other creative ways to achieve primary and any secondary objectives, all maps having additional badges/challenges providing some replay value. These challenges range from things such as only using certain characters to complete the mission, speedruns, not using any cover, and several other ways to push you to find another way through the mission.

Each of the 5 characters is well thought out, Hayato has a shuriken and is able to distract enemies by throwing stones, basically the all-rounder of the team. Mugen is the strong man able to take down multiple enemies in one attack, but also able to carry bodies and lure enemy units with his bottle of sake. Then there’s Yuki, able to lure enemy units with her trap and whistle. Aiko uses disguises to distract and lure enemy units. Lastly there’s Takuma who acts as the team sniper, able to target enemy units at long range.

The difficulty levels seem well done with beginner being the easiest, normal, and hardcore level being the hardest. Difficulty is ramped up by adding some additional enemies to the map, changing out simple guards for tougher NPC’s (Strawhats/Samurai), or NPC’s that can’t be distracted (Strawhats/Samurai).

Graphics and sound are excellent, they’ve really done a great job of creating a believable Japanese world that looks and feels like feudal Japan, lots of beautiful trees and flowers, streams and lakes, lush green fields, snow, the maps are stunning and very pleasing on the eye. When walking on snow you’ll leave footprints behind which can be used by enemies to track you down, or by you as a tool to lure enemy units in for you to kill. You’ll also get visual queues indicating how much noise your actions will make, allowing you to decide when to get noisy and when to keep it quiet.

Alarms system is also good, rather than the entire map going on alert if you get spotted, as it did in Commandos, in this game there are separate sectors/zones where an alarm is triggered, so only that part of the map goes on alert, with additional enemies being deployed.

Controls, I never had any issues with the controls in this game, and if you dislike the default key binds you can always change them to whatever you prefer. Sometimes there can be small issues where a view cone is not 100% accurate, but in my experience, this occurs in all games in this genre, but I would stress this is a very minor issue and 99% of the time the view cones work perfectly. The showdown mode is also excellent, allowing you to easily plan out actions for each of your team members so you can take down multiple enemy units in one go.

Bugs, well there really isn’t much to say here, there are a few minor issues I’ve noticed, but on the whole, Mimimi have put out some high-quality games with very few bugs, and Shadow Tactics is no exception.

I think for me one of the big reasons I’ve loved all the games from Mimimi in this genre is the fact that they focused on something other than WW2, and the vast majority of games in this genre do focus on WW2. This fact only makes it all the more sad that Mimimi have stopped making games, at least for now, and there are very few developers that strived for the level of quality that Mimimi did, a developer I will very much miss.

In summary, again, I would highly recommend this game to anyone. Great visuals, great sound, good controls, good story, a very enjoyable game.

[h3][b][i]Buy it. Play it. Love it.[/i][/b][/h3]
I was fortunate to get the opportunity to play and review [i]Mimimi Games' Desperados III[/i] shortly after it was released in 2020. It brought back fun memories of a wee Slav playing [i]Commandos[/i] and [i]Robin Hood[/i] on his PC with MBs of RAM. And after idly sitting in my library, collecting e-dust, I finally played [i]Shadow Tactics[/i], [i]Mimimi Games'[/i] first Real-Time Tactics (RTT) game. So, I went backwards. Thus, I expected some missteps.

Still, I thoroughly enjoyed myself and decided, after 100%-ing it, to author this review.
Enjoy.

[h3][b][i]Wow, Japan![/i][/b][/h3]
The story is predictable and bland. But I liked the Shogun's blades sent to quell this "mysterious" baddie's rebellion. They had chemistry, and the seldom banter was entertaining. Most importantly, they had compelling motivation to seek the carotid arteries of the main baddie. So, I was a little invested.

But let's move on to the presentation. Spoiler — [b]it's excellent.[/b]

I'm just a sucker for Edo period Japanese aesthetic. Level environments are rich in detail despite the birds-eye perspective and a low polygon-ish look. The same love and attention to detail were bestowed upon the enemy units and our sneaky blades. So, zoom in when you can and treat your eyes. The soundtrack acts as a stunning minstrel of the visuals, following it everywhere, composing fitting tunes that amplify the atmosphere and take the presentation to greater heights. And the main theme... all the right spots were hit. It starts very manly and powerful, making you feel like a big boy wearing his big boy pants, only to abruptly nosedive into the emotional abyss, bending you over its knee and slapping you silly. Shame it wasn't to [i]Shadow Tactics[/i] what [i]Warthog Run[/i] was to [i]Halo 3[/i] — [b]a banger curtain closer.[/b]

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2962615463

Anyway... What's the deal with those sound effects?

Since dealing death is a large part of what you'll do, the many pertaining to those actions needed to be glorious. And by Joe, they are. I especially adored how Yuki's trap sings when someone (un)fortunate steps on it. Reminds me of a melon being penetrated. As for them voices, I will share with you the sage advice bestowed unto me — [b]please, do not the dub.[/b] It's not [i]South Park[/i] Engrish, but it's close. Yuki sometimes even sounds British?!

Lastly, the UI. Besides some pesky context actions like jumping off a ledge being consistently inconsistent, it's flawless. You get all the vital information about your enemies, the environment and the mission objective with a few clicks.

But guess what? The previous giant wall of text doesn't matter. Well, it does, but it doesn't. You feel me? This following wall of text matters. It's about the most crucial element for me, my aboki — [b]the gameplay.[/b]

[h3][b][i]I can finally be NINJA!!![/i][/b][/h3]
The gameplay loop in RTT games has something special that makes me giddy when I play them. It feels eerily similar to the [i]Hitman[/i] franchise, at least on the surface. While you don't get a bald man to play with, there's a meaty level (in size), which feels like a maze, with many paths, twists and turns, offering plenty of choices on how to reach the finish line. And being sneaky is what the RTT gameplay is all about. So, don't raise alarms, and stay out of sight by navigating past the [b]enemy's viewcone.[/b] You can do that by causing a distraction or affecting the range of the enemy viewcone with hero abilities, giving you a couple of seconds to act and slip past unnoticed. But maps are also littered with objects. They can be used as cover, with you crouching past the enemy's gaze, staying within the stripped viewcone lines these covers produce.

Sadly, compared to [i]Desperados III[/i], there is less environmental interactivity and more linearity. And with [b]knocked-out guards waking up, potentially causing (un)happy little accidents[/b], a blind hardcore non-lethal playthrough was impossible.
Thus, I just [b]killed everyone.[/b]

So, let's meet the reapers — Yuki, Mugen, Hayato, Aiko, Takuma, and their [i]kawaii[/i] [b]tanuki[/b], Kuma. Together they form the cadaverous blades of the Shogun.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2951343632

Each possesses a particular set of skills you must master to wiggle your way around the maze-like levels [i]Mimimi Games[/i] prepared for you.

At the very top of the food chain sits [b]Yuki.[/b] Don't let her fragile, slender frame fool you — [b]she a certified beast[/b], capable of sending anyone to meet the white-bearded dude up on the clouds. Slightly below is [b]Mugen[/b], the thicc samurai daddy. His hobbies include carrying heavy stuff, slicing enemy samurai and using his overpowered area-of-effect skill against regular enemy units for crowd control. While his thiccness means there is more of him to love, it also makes him slower, unable to swim and jump off ledges. The knees can only endure so much before they tap out.

Then there is [b]Hayato[/b], the grumpy shinobi, who can do a bit of everything — [b]distracting the enemy's attention + decent close/ranged combat ability[/b]. As for [b]Aiko[/b], Mugen's kunoichi sweetheart, she's well-versed in the cosplay arts, allowing her to move freely across the map. But enemy samurai will see through her guise, so be mindful of their gaze. And whilst cosplaying, she can take advantage of the horny guard's gaze, focusing it solely on her by engaging in small talk. Sadly, like Hayato, Aiko can only distract guards from looking at a particular spot.

And then we have [b]Takuma[/b]. A skilled marksman with an affinity for gunpowder and bombs that go [b]BOOOM![/b] But having attacks with limited ammo due to his love affair with gunpowder, noisy running courtesy of his wooden leg, and inability to swim/move bodies make his limitations detrimental for a solo act. [b]Kuma[/b], his fluffy tanuki, does accompany him and can distract/lure enemies wherever you desire. So, that's nice.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2962913904

Overall, the blades felt less balanced than Cooper's gang in [i]Desperados III[/i] — [b]there's a clear line between a Top G and NPC.[/b] But besides this balance shenanigans, the [b]Shadow Mode[/b] here pales when compared to the one in [i]Desperados III[/i]. You can still plan and execute one action per character simultaneously. However, it [b]doesn't freeze the game while you plan your attack.[/b] Thus, expect mistakes and reloading, as you'll mainly use it against moving targets in groups of two or more units.

And before we part ways, I want to voice my only [b]real[/b] issue with the game — [b]no proper level where all five blades jointly act.[/b] I was teased, toyed with, and led to believe daddy was feasting tonight! But my climax must have gotten lost in the mail because this vapid finale was definitely not it. Compared to [i]Desperados III[/i], [i]Shadow Tactics[/i] royally disappoints here.

But hey, you don't learn to walk without bruising your kneecaps a bit. So, some mistakes were to be expected from [i]Mimimi Games[/i] as they dipped their toes in the RTT genre with [i]Shadow Tactics[/i]. Surprisingly, the poor climax of a drab and predictable plot, hero (un)balance, and no level that unleashes all of them together did little to ruin my overall enjoyment. My love for the genre's entertaining gameplay loop didn't allow it. Splash excellent group chemistry, stunning visuals and a banger soundtrack on top, and my enjoyment was only stroked further.

I haven't really played a stealth game before, but Shadow Tactics was an excellent introduction to the genre. The sprawling maps feel tightly designed, each a gordian knot to slowly pick apart guard by guard, or simply cut right through with an ingenious strategy. The game obviously has intended routes for you to take, supported by specific interactibles and set pieces, but there are usually multiple and the missions are very open-ended. While at the beginning it was enough to simply slink out of the shadows and then return to them for each successive kill, by the end it can become quite intense, requiring a number of connected moves pulled off in order to make things work. This leads to a very heavy reliance on quicksaving, which the game takes in stride, even popping up an alert on screen if you haven't quicksaved in the past minute.

My only real problem is the camera. It is fixed to awkward angles (though I later found a horizontal free move keybind, the vertical angle is still horrendous at times), making it difficult to actually see what is going on in more cramped spaces, and occasionally being almost nauseating when dealing with certain areas.

Every action has a consequence - if I set a trap *here* it will affect *this* set of guards, but how will the nearby civilians react? The art style is really attractive, the voice acting is top notch, and the soundtrack is phenomenal - the combination really transports you to the game's world. I played through the original game twice, the second time incorporating the Aiko's Choice expansion (which takes place in the middle of the original game), and I might dabble in a third playthrough one of these days, once my game backlog is a little better. If you like the challenge of strategizing an entire mission and overcoming all obstacles in your path, this game is for you!

If you're seeking a challenging and strategic game, then this is the game for you. Even game developers have taken into consideration those who crave greater challenges, incorporating an achievement with 117 unique challenges. In summary, it stands as one of the finest intellectual games available, and I highly recommend giving it a try.

[h1]An Essential Strategy/Stealth/Puzzle Game For Almost Everyone[/h1] 
Shadow Tactics on paper seems like a niche title for a very particular group of strategy nerds. In reality it is more akin to something like Portal - enjoyable for almost everyone - just not something you realized you'd like until you try it.

[h1]The Good + The Bad[/h1]
Shadow Tactics is a real-time tactical stealth strategy game that functions almost like a puzzle game in the way you manipulate multiple characters to perform specific actions at key moments with the purpose of achieving a given mission objective on each of about a dozen maps. 

It's pointless to go into heavy detail about the actual moment to moment game-play but Shadow Tactics introduces the mechanics slowly and builds confidence in the player while at the same time gradually increasing the challenge. It is one of the most perfectly balanced, paced, and user friendly 'strategy' games you'll ever play. It's the best kind of strategy game that excites you with its mechanics and game-play while leaving you with the desire to master its challenges and optional objectives. 

From map to map the game also has a paralleling narrative with corresponding voice over narration. The voice work is simply outstanding while the narrative is engaging and adds just the right amount of punctuation and spice to the strategy game-play. The music is pitch perfect giving an authentic feel to the Japanese setting. The graphics and UI are tightly designed and timeless in their aesthetic choices.

So what then is there to complain about? The answer is almost nothing. While for me the gradual ramp up in challenge from map to map was perfect, others' experiences may very. In those scenarios it would have been nice if there were a bit more generosity with character voice overs to give the player tips or suggestions on how best to approach a given map objective. As is, there are some hints included and it's easy enough to search for a YouTube walk-through. But I can imagine a certain type of player getting frustrated easily if the solution is not more accessible to them. Also the puzzle like nature of each map objective means there isn't an endless array of ways to achieve the objective. Objectives aren't singular in their solutions but they may not be as open-ended as some may like. Overall these are minor criticisms in an otherwise perfect game and fundamentally comes down to individual preference over being attributable to bad design.  

[h1]Technical[/h1]
[list]
[*]Stunningly rock solid fps performance.
[*]Zero crashes or performance issues.
[*]Can run on most potato PCs
[/list]

[h1]Bottom Line[/h1]
Shadow Tactics is an 'S'-tier game. A modern classic. Easy to jump into and rewarding to master. Something anyone that considers themselves open to different types of games should play - especially if there's any type of game you like that is even vaguely strategy-based or puzzle-like (Magic the Gathering, Civilization, Portal, etc). On sale there is little risk to buying the game and a worthy addition to most people's libraries.

- The story is what I would call "nicely done". It's not a literature masterpiece by any means, which is not a bad thing at all. It's interesting enough to make you feel interested, and the characters all have their own appeal. I admit, some of the dialogues could be delivered better. The characters are quirky and a little cringy at times, but I feel like that's part of the charm. I actually found myself emotionally invested towards the characters, especially towards the later half of the game. Can't lie, the ending made me kinda sad for a bit lmao

- The gameplay is what you'd expect from a stealth strategy game. I really liked stealth, but I have also never played any strategy games, especially RTS. And this game gave me the best introduction to the genre. By the end of the game, I can't help but feel excited to play more games just like Shadow Tactics. It's exactly what I wanted in a stealth game. Observation, tactical planning, decision making, and execution. It feels so damn satisfying when you take your time to craft a plan, execute it, fail, refining your strategy, and finally succeeding in the end. It's like playing chess, or solving an elaborate puzzle.

- The characters all have their own sets of tools and traits which can be combined to tackle an obstacle, but sometimes there are levels where one character is clearly better than the others, and can be used for every situation. Though this is not a fatal flaw, since you can choose to be more creative with your approach. On my first playthrough, i rarely used Takuma, feeling him to be a liability due to his weaknesses, but on my second playthrough, I found myself using him more, which in turn helped me discover more creative ways to solve a level. Because that's what the game is all about. Creative problem solving! 

There are some clear flaws, though. The camera and controls. The camera can become awkward or downright frustrating, especially at the far edges of levels. The controls, while manageable, can sometimes feel clunky and unresponsive. For example, if you click on an unreachable spot, your characters will stop moving entirely, which could lead to detections. Similarly, moving multiple characters to a single location can cause them to collide, slowing down their movement or even exposing one of them unintentionally. The shadow mode is also a bit underwhelming, and I usually only found myself using them when I'm just trying to be fancy with my tactics. Because of the enemies' pathing and predictable viewcones, sometimes all you need is time and patience. If you don't mind taking it slow, you can finish some levels without ever using shadow mode. 

[h3] Summary [/h3]
[b] Gameplay: 8/10. [/b] Good level design, lots of opportunities to make different plans and strategies. Wonky camera and controls which takes some time getting used to.
[b] Story: 8/10. [/b] Very good. Characters are interesting, and the story is simple but sweet.
[b] Visuals: 9/10. [/b] Very appealing aesthetics and visuals. Game graphics look timeless, probably will still look good in the year 2050.
[b] Replayability: 7/10. [/b] The level stays the same, but the badges and achievements urges you to replay the game, but with different gameplans and approach.

At the time of this review, I have played 10 missions, all on the hardest difficulty (which I think is the most realistic mode in terms of the enemy Ai). I stopped after having finished mission 10 and moved on to play Partisans 1941 from the same publisher which I enjoyed much more. But it doesn't mean that this game isn't good. In fact it is very good but due to a few limitations it starts to feel repetitive after passing Mission 6 or 7 such as the limitation of the era itself (Edo period) when you mostly fight with melee weapons, strictly linear missions and paths (but you can be creative on your approach), and you can bring only up to 2 - 3 characters max in most missions (only 1 or 2 missions you get to bring all 5 characters but still get separated into two teams) which is a major missed opportunity in the game because if you are allowed to bring all 5 characters more often you could be more creative in your approach and the game would not feel this much repetitive. 

But I understand that the developer tried to make the game as difficult as possible to challenge the players. But they forgot that they could still make the game hard while allowing all 5 characters by adding more enemy soldiers and/or complexity of the objectives. Not to mention the replayability. 

Playing this game, in a way, you clearly see the developer's attempt to block your way to victory because you see how the enemy soldiers are carefully placed in a way that they think no flies will ever get in without being noticed but they deliberately force you to go or use a certain path in order to pass which limits player's creativity 

Fortunately, there is little to no frustration playing this game even though you find yourself dead or caught 5 times at the same spot because it allows unlimited quick saves. So before you do anything risky you can quick save and retry after you have learned what went wrong, unless you forgot to quick save. 

However, if you are careful and plan well enough, it's likely that you won't die. Most of the times I died when I forgot to switch between characters, for instance, I thought I was controlling the ninja but actually I was controlling the girl, so I was moving the wrong character and got her killed.       

Will I come back to finish this game? Yes for sure I will come back after a while. 

Do I recommend this game? Certainly yes if you like this kind of games or finding out. But maybe with a discount, because Partisans 1941 is much better in all aspects.

Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun is a really solid stealth game with a fair amount of tactical/strategy elements, and I really enjoyed playing it for a few weeks on my Steam Deck. Where most stealth games use more of a first-person or a third-person view and concentrate on a single character or maybe a pair of characters, Shadow Tactics takes a larger isometric view of the map and uses squads of 2-5 characters with varying special abilties. I really enjoyed that this large-scale vision allows you plan an approach towards your mission goals, especially in conjunction with its planning/execution system. Shadow Tactics allows you to plan and set up moves to be executed at the same time, so that a character who is in disguise and talking to a pair of guards can stab one guard while a second character sneaks up and stabs the other guard, while a third character throws a shuriken at the guard on a rooftop who might see the other two getting ganked. This really enables a lot of skillful tactical planning and execution, presenting you with both difficult challenges to figure out how to approach, and a reasonably wide variety of skills to try to resolve those challenges. 

The game's story wasn't anything special, but I did enjoy the presentation, especially the animated scenes between each mission. There was one particular scene when the entire squad is reunited that I thought was particularly impactful, aided by how the scene physically unfolds. I would've been interested to see some gameplay mechanics that maybe tied into how you decided to accomplish each mission, perhaps making your decisions a bit more impactful in subsequent missions. Absent any such impacts, I just played the whole game as a full-on murder machine, making sure none of my foes lived through any mission. There was one particular vignette that occurred during the mission at an invaded village that I went far out of my way to try to prevent from happening, and I was pretty disappointed that the game didn't support my heroic intervention. Adding some minor elements like this could've really helped elevate the game, to add "small stories" to the game's larger narrative. 

Shadow Tactics was a fairly difficult game, even on "Normal" difficulty mode, which did make it a little grind-y at times. Overall though, I think its a really good addition to both the stealth and the tactical strategy genres. The core gameplay loop of watching, planning, and trying to pull off your plan works really well, especially because the game generally makes it very easy to try again (at least on Normal difficulty) if something goes wrong. I've always enjoyed the watch/plan/execute cycle in other stealth/assassination games, but the squad-based strategy element really elevated the gameplay here. If you enjoy either of the stealth or strategy genres, I think you'll find Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun to be worth your while, especially if you're playing on the Steam Deck.

Shadow Tactics shines on multiple fronts. On its highest difficulty, the game offers a formidable challenge, demanding precise planning and execution, which feels incredibly rewarding when mastered. The beautifully crafted story immerses you in feudal Japan, brought to life by diverse, visually stunning locations that range from snowy villages to sprawling castles. The Japanese voice acting is a standout, enhancing the game's authentic and atmospheric vibe. Highly recommended for fans of stealth and strategy!

This is the most satisfying stealth game I've ever played. A vivid setting and time period, combined with the elegant ability to synchronize actions of up to 5 characters (each with varied abilities and shortcomings), creates an experience that requires creativity, finesse, and attention to detail.

The things that make Shadow Tactics great are the difficulty and level variety. Each mission presents new challenges for you to ponder, such as footprints in the snow, torches that expose your movements at night, or the sudden loss of characters and equipment you've come to rely upon. These things force you to get creative, encourage you to adapt and refine your playstyle, and reward you for thinking outside the box. Enemies are quite competent, even on normal difficulty, eliminating the cop-out option of forsaking stealth and going in guns blazing. And while each level is more-or-less linear, there are always multiple ways to go about completing your mission, including some the game leaves for you to discover on your own.

I love a game that rewards experimentation, doesn't hold your hand, and requires the patience and persistence to see your plans through. This game excels at all these, set against the exquisite backdrop of feudal Japan. The fact that you can grab it at 90% discount makes it a no-brainer. Lastly, for a truly immersive feel, I highly recommend playing with the Japanese voiceovers. In my opinion they exceed the quality of the English voices, if you don't mind reading subtitles.

I recommend both Mimimi Game's Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun and Desperados 3 as excellent additions in the stealth RTS genre, in line with the memorable Commandos series and Spellbound Entertainment's Desperados 1 and 2.

Upon first playing Shadow Tactics and Desperados 3 it might feel same-y to its predecessors with their same-y view cone mechanics, but if you made the mistake of trying to replay the Commandos or Desperados 1 & 2 for the sake of comparison, you’d lose a lot of the nostalgic reverence you had for them because ST and D3 does improve a lot in terms of both gameplay, and presentation.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
If you have never played one of these before: in every level/chapter you load into a relatively large map with guards whose locations and patrol paths are predetermined, you are given a certain combination of characters with their specific toolsets to play with, and you basically spend most of the time avoiding the guards’ view cones, while utilizing your characters’ toolset to remove/distract the guards in order to reach the objective’s destination on the map to progress (with tons of quicksaves and quickloads in between).

I love the optional challenges given after the first completion of a level, which are a great way of incentivizing repeat plays with different strategies and goals in mind. Though you do lose a lot of the level replay incentive upon finishing all the goals, there’s still a fair amount of entertainment value in a game without infinite replayability.

Compared to its predecessors, ST and D3 have optimized a more streamlined control scheme for the modern era with character abilities accessible with asdfg/qwert keys (customizable in options), as opposed to Commando’s insistence to use the entire alphabet list. Characters and abilities feel as fun and well balanced as they were, with good map design which gradually becomes more challenging. I remember being able to cheese Desperados 1 by revealing your position on a rooftop and unloading your party’s bullets on all enemies who climb up a ladder 1 by 1, severely limiting ammunition for guns in ST and D3 was a good call.

[h1]Presentation[/h1]
Both ST and D3 makes great use of their respective time period settings (Edo Japan/Wild west) beautifully, with well-detailed levels, decently likeable characters and engaging story. It isn’t particularly fair to compare the visuals to games from two decades ago but it does have gorgeous visuals, with Shadow Tactics: Blade of the Shogun being the stand out in particular, probably because its Edo period setting allows for more prettier architectural designs and environments compared to the stereotypically brown dusty aesthetic of the Wild West or the olive-green military bases aesthetic of World War 2. Love the big city night levels in both ST (Matsuyama City) and D3 (New Orleans) in particular.

[h1]Story[/h1]
In Edo period Japan, the Shogun brought peace to Japan by winning the war. However, some conspire against the shogun to plunge the country back into strife and usurp power. In order to thwart this plot, the Shogun's most trusted samurai retainer assembles four other companions to sabotage these rebels and uncover the mastermind hiding in the shadows (literally calling himself "The Shadow" in Japanese) and bring him to justice.

The game's plot is told through in-engine cutscenes between missions and character conversations in the midst of a level. The plot is pretty standard fare, with very predictable plot twists. While the main plot isn't really anything to write home about, the main characters are pretty endearing and fun to hear bantering with each other. The Japanese voiceover is also stellar.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Shadow Tactics is an isometric real time tactics game with 13 missions. You control a team of five characters from a top down perspective against a map full of baddies. Each character comes with a pre-defined set of items/abilities: a melee weapon (or sniper rifle), a unique ability, a distraction option, a handicraft pistol, and a bandage set. Although that doesn't sound like a lot of variety, each character has their nuances with the items available to them. For example, one character may distract enemies by throwing a rock and only getting them to turn away for a few seconds, while a different character might send a trained raccoon dog to make cute noises to get all the enemies preoccupied asking the important question - who's a good boy? Some characters are nimble and can climb vines are grapple to the top of a building with a hookshot, while others require conventional ladders. Some characters can pick up enemy bodies (a certain powerhouse can even carry two for the price of one and just throw them onto other enemies!), while the less brawny characters can only slowly drag them on the ground, and some can't move bodies at all. So you always have to consider which character is best for a specific job in a specific situation.

While you technically can go on a frontal assault, your characters don't have much in the way of ranged options, so you can easily get outnumbered and killed if you don't keep a low profile. Although classified as a stealth game, you'll find that it's more of a puzzle game: figuring out how to take out how to take out Soldier A without being seen by Soldier B or C, who either have direct line of sight on Soldier A, or are supposed to regularly meet up with them and will get suspicious if Soldier A is running late. Oftentimes, figuring out how to get through a segment will result in spamming F5 and F8 until you get it just right, but at least the quickloads are fast. Usually, there's more than one way to get the job done, and even more than one route to take to your goal. Your mileage per level can vary anywhere from 2-4 hours if you're meticulous and take your time, to 1-5 minute speedruns when you figure out the most optimal path. Nearly every level comes with some new gimmick to make things more interesting, and each level comes with 9 bonus challenges (badges) for some extra replay value.

TL;DR: An interesting, well-executed niche game that doesn't quite change things up enough to stay exciting over its full runtime.[hr][/hr]
I'd never played a stealth tactics game before Shadow Tactics. I picked it up a long time ago after reading very positive reviews, but never got around to it. I played it in 2024 to see if I enjoyed the genre, as Artificer’s (the developers of ShowGunners) Sumerian Six has me curious.

The story is set during the early Edo era in Japanese history, a nascent period of stability following over a hundred years of civil wars. Your team of characters serves the Shogun, and is tasked with upholding the fragile peace. Each character is 100% trope with no further development, and the Big Bad is shockingly the only named nobleman that has been introduced other than the Shogun. In short, I think the developers enjoyed the idea of using the setting to deliver a specific style of gameplay, and weren't overly concerned with delivering a unique narrative. It's fine, though I would've really preferred the voice actors not bother with the cheesy faux-Japanese accents.

Your goals vary per mission, but always involve maneuvering your rotating band of characters stealthily through an enemy-infested map. The game is played in an isometric view, giving you a bird's-eye view of the action. There is no fog of war, so you can always see all enemies, but you can only actively monitor one foe’s field of view at a time. This is smart, as otherwise I could see players being driven to just play the UI, rather than carefully focusing their attention. You swap between characters freely, and each has unique abilities to lure enemies, temporarily blind them, or otherwise facilitate shadowy murder.

As you advance you'll be facing different enemy types in more complex configurations, and you'll need to puzzle out solutions where your ninjas work in unison. The problem is that this is a real-time game, and you can only control one character at a time. The game’s answer is Shadow Mode; when activated you can map out a single action per character that can then be executed simultaneously. This is pretty cool, but also fairly limited. Since you can literally only queue a single action, you could have each character kill a guard, but then your characters will just stand around until you individually direct them to hide bodies and/or themselves. It's fairly awkward, especially since Shadow Mode doesn't pause time to let you immediately move on to your next step. Happily, the game relies heavily on quick-saving, and quick-loading is super-fast, which gives you the freedom to try out plenty of different tactics with near-zero consequence for failure.

If you enjoy yourself, you'll be delighted with all the extra optional objectives the game presents. These involve killing key enemies in unique ways, finding special map secrets, and other fun little distractions. I could see myself getting wrapped up in these, but unfortunately each level also features a speedrun objective, so I knew I'd never get them all (I personally hate speedrunning). This led to a hard pass by my completionist brain, but your mileage may vary. 

My major gripe with this otherwise excellent title is that it can get pretty repetitive. There are only three types of enemies, and though your team makeup is different each mission, and there tend to be a few map-specific flourishes, you'll eventually find yourself using essentially the same tactics over and over. Additionally, there is no character progression or customization on offer, so you can't really tailor your characters to suit your preferred play style.

Overall, I had a good deal of fun with Shadow Tactics, and it makes me a little sad that the developer Mimimi closed its doors recently. I can see myself dipping back into this genre occasionally despite being absolutely awful at traditional real-time strategy games, but I don't see it becoming a major staple of my gaming diet.

Every guard is watched by at least one other guard. Killing guards becomes a process of tediously killing your way through an entire section of the map just so you can kill one guard that was blocking a gate.

For a stealth tactics game, the maps are also shockingly linear. Sure, it's open, but there's only one path that doesn't lead to certain death. After a time, you get the impression that every map has one main designed path with a few shortcuts, and every area, every section of the map is just a puzzle to solve (and time correctly). I didn't once feel like I could experiment with using different combinations of abilities, or one mission, going vertical, or going sneaking on another. I can't count the number of times I thought "Oh, I'd have loved to have this character right now, I wonder how I could use his explosive with her powder.." etc. except that every mission has a specific loadout of characters. I never felt like I had a creative choice in my use of abilities or characters. And even with the characters you get, working together is pointless. Even the abilities each character has seems unnecessarily limited. Only one character can throw rocks? Only one character can make a luring noise? It's arbitrary decisions like this that make the gameplay uncreative.

The squad mechanics are almost non-existent. I found myself playing most of the maps one character at a time, only changing when I faced a situation that required a different character's abilities. You can only control one character at a time, except to move, and even then it's a disaster because they all have different movement speeds and collide with each other constantly, frequently catching the guards' attention. The only way to use your characters together is using "shadow mode" which allows you to queue actions from different characters so you can execute them at once. HOWEVER, shadow mode only allows you to queue up ONE ACTION per character, making complex planning (i.e. shadow TACTICS) virtually excluded by design. The game wants you to control characters and make decisions in real-time, but making real-time decisions is impossible because the maps are crawling with guards, and this is not a combat game. If you're spotted by a guard, game over is all but certain. Reinforcements begin to shoot from afar, you cannot fight more than one guard, you cannot run, you cannot become invisible. Even if you do manage to escape, the entire map will be on alert, making the rest of the mission nearly impossible. And your other characters CANNOT HELP AT ALL because again, REAL TIME. If you're spotted, your sniper can't take out the guard, your heavy can't clear the guards, because without that action-planning, by the time you switch to them, it's too late. The game becomes about timing, waiting and save-scumming over and over to get characters across the map, one by one.

That brings me to the save-scumming. It's included in the gameplay by design, even going as far as to include a timer reminding you to constantly save. Some others don't mind this, but I personally found it frustrating and flow-breaking. The game relies on save-scumming because it's the only way the player can time moves perfectly enough to succeed because the stealth, squad teamwork, and combat mechanics are not effective enough alone because they can't be properly planned and executed. It makes the gameplay tedious, and when it collides with the controls, it becomes truly frustrating.

The majority of the game relies on the mouse, and a few clunky hotkeys. Switching between characters takes too long to perform actions across characters in real-time. Executing actions, however, is the true nail in the coffin. I can't count the number of times I've clicked on a guard to kill them, and instead, without my realizing, the kill skill wasn't toggled, and my character walks right up to the guard and sits there, waiting for death. Me too, buddy. Or that I thought I clicked on the ground but instead clicked on a wall, and then my character walks out in front of a guard, reload the save. Or, that I had the wrong character selected, and again, ruined the play. The camera is not suitable for the amount of tight spaces and vertical elements in the game. You can't look top down, and rotating the camera requires stopping whatever else you're doing.

All these elements combine to make the gameplay an absolute grind that discourages tactical gameplay in favor of save-scumming over and over to solve precision timing situations. Wan

I returned the game, as it was not what I expected. First, let me say there is a suspicious amount of uncritical reviews, so be weary of that. Second, this game is not really a squad based tactics game, but a puzzle game with a medieval Japanese theme. Lastly, take my review with a grain of salt since I only played the first two missions.

The reason it is a puzzle game is because there seems to be one path plotted by the developers. The developers box you into figuring out how to kill these set guards before you move can move onto the next area, rinse repeat. I mean, if you like puzzle games, then it is great for you. However I expected a squad based tactics game. It really breaks the immersion once you realize there is a set sequence of specific actions to perform.

Next, it really is not a squad based game. Sure, you can command multiple characters, and set them to take specific actions at the same time. However, the limited nature of the levels means you are just figuring out what the game wants you to do. Moreover, you command one character at a time, and can only use the squad mechanic to take ONE action with each character. It does not feel innovative, and again, is just an easy puzzle game.

Next, the story did not hook me within the first two missions, but at least some of the characters were interesting. Some characters die on the alter of medieval Japanese tropes, but others, namely the old man, are really interesting. The story regrettably did not hook me at all, and maybe that would have changed, but the game does not really wow within the first hour and a half. It just seemed like, insert some stereotypical medieval plot. Maybe there is more too it, but I will never get the chance to know.

Lastly, for a unity engine game, the art design was quite nice. Maybe I would have wished for better use of shadows, but the colors all seem to pop well. The design also communicates things quickly to the player, without sacrificing immersion. The medieval Japanese theme is also executed really well. 

Ultimately, this game was just not fun. I had more fun writing this review than playing the game. Steam recommends it to me because I love tactical games, but this was not a tactical game. You spend the whole time figuring out which specific ability, in what spot, and at what time, the game wants you to use, which is a puzzle. I expect a real tactical game to allow me to approach a situation with multiple choices, with maybe some of those choices being less optimal. Moreover, I also expect to be able to make more complicated actions than  "use x ability at the same time,," also with multiple characters, to be able to call it a squad game. This game forces you to go down one path, especially on the harder difficulty, which is why it is a puzzle game and not a squad based tactics game.

If you like big medieval Japanese puzzles, go knock yourself out, if not, then I would pass.

As others have stated, there are many abilities that could easily be shared by different characters, but aren't, in order to artificially limit player choice. 

For example: 
[list]
[*] The Samurai can heave a heavy barrel onto a roof, but not throw a pebble to distract his enemies. 
[*] The ninja assassin only has [i]one[/i] shuriken.
[*]  The ninja  assassin has exactly [b]zero[/b] decoys, but the samurai does.
[/list]

Makes sense. Now, if any character could do anything, then they'd be boring and interchangeable. However, some overlap should still exist. In games like XCOM, this is dealt with in a more sensical fashion: almost anyone can throw a grenade, but some will not be accurate, or not have much range. That approach is far superior.

What really got me is that the only way that the game becomes a little more interesting is by trying to complete both general, and mission specific challenges, not the objectives. For example, there's one challenge that states that you should kill no one other than the target in any given mission.That makes it difficult to complete a level, for sure. Maybe impossible for some, idk as I haven't played enough. But having to artificially limiting my own actions in order to make the game more interesting, is a sign of poor design. 

Another thing that bothered me is the terrible camera control. It's difficult to grasp all the different paths to an objective without rotating the camera [b]often[/b], and having to press ALT, while also switching characters, etc. is annoying. Add the contextual actions (CTRL + Click to drop a body in a bush), and it gets annoying. 

One more I'll add is that the character AI is pretty dumb. Often, if you tell them to reach a certain point, and they have to say, go through a door to get there, or jump down a ledge, they won't perform the action without your explicit instructions. Makes ferrying the team over to a given spot an annoying chore.

At the end of the day, this game simply did not "spark joy". Playing it felt vaguely chore-like.

Given the positive reviews, I didn't expect ST:BotS to come off as poorly as it did. 

First, it controls clunkily, an issue that goes beyond keybinding (though why the game defaults to left-click movement, God only knows). If a tactical game insists on real-time play, then it should take notes from the RTS games that pioneered the field. Yet ST:BotS won't let players click-and-drag to select units or move multiple units at a time, a lack painfully obvious in the first tutorial mission. 

Then, there's the issue of poor information management. For a game that wants the player to move precisely w/r/t guards' FOVs, then one should have the option to see those guards' vision cones by default. Yet strangely, the game makes the player right-click on individual guards to see what they see and won't show multiple guards' FOVs, despite every level containing multiple guards. 

Finally, this game doesn't even attempt to make the stealth game's cock-up cascade fun to play, actively encouraging the player to quicksave and quickload if something goes wrong.

Perhaps a sequel will correct these issues in control and gameplay. Until they're resolved, I cannot recommend this game.

The quick save feature, while brilliant in theory, just leads you to resent the game's level design even more. Expecting a player to bash their head against a wall over and over and clearly designing the game around that process is just not fun design. Overcoming challenging obstacles is a rewarding experience, I don't think anyone would challenge that claim. There are hundreds of games that exemplify this well.
