So... Shadow Tactics is a good game, well-put-together, as long as you know what to expect. Don't expect a squad-based tactics game, and don't expect a stealth game, either. Expect a puzzle game, played out with multiple pieces, with stealth mechanics as a veneer to cover the puzzles.

Also, expect a game designed to take advantage of quicksave/quickload. This is a game where you often need to make several things happen at once in a sequence of perfect timing, but there's no way to pause the game to issue commands or plan out your moves. You are expected to have to retry the same puzzle several times until you can get the timing just right. 

Unfortunately, getting to that point involves quite a bit of waiting, and that waiting drags on even longer if you're not making liberal use of the quicksave button. This is a game where you might spend several minutes getting from point A to point B, just to spend another ten minutes trying to get the timing perfect, and now you've managed to complete one small part of the larger puzzle. Most of these levels take over an hour to complete, despite the fact that you could run across them inside of 30 seconds. 

I really wanted to like this, but it takes all of the negatives of stealth games (lots of waiting, high consequences for failure, often hidden enemies), multiplies them by adding in the difficulties of planning and execution in real-time and with multiple characters, and doesn't give you the control that usually is a necessity in either the action or squad-based tactics games. As a result, the game often feels frustrating to me and I feel like it's wasting my time.

If you enjoy pure logic puzzles with a stealth theme, you might love this. Pathfinding is utter trash. For example, I wanted the two ninjas to drop down from the ledge and knife two guards while old man shoots a third. Impossible because they have to drop down via hook shot first, even though ledges of the same or greater height can be dropped down from elsewhere in the game. Throwing rocks are almost entirely useless and for some reason this ninja carries exactly ONE shuriken. Which leads me to the next thing: Shadow Mode.

Shadow mode is terrible. Unlike in Desperados, it does not pause the game. This renders it basically useless but many situations are of course set up where you need multiple things to happen at once. I suspect this was intended to make it "challenging" but it really just is inefficient and tedious; especially since only the fat Samurai is capable of taking out multiple enemies at one time and only via melee. Further, you can only issue the command to run and attack in Shadow Mode if the enemy is close by. This is inexcusable and makes no sense whatsoever. In Desperados, Showdown Mode feels rewarding because you can plan ahead multiple actions per character and then make a complex plan work. Here, you feel happy when they just did what you fing wanted the first time.

Speaking of tedious things: The game lacks a fast-forward key. So you can just sit and wait forever.

Characters also have abilities unsuited to their specific attributes; this was remedied in desperados 3 whereby the equivalent characters had abilities swapped around and some added. It makes more sense that a fast character like Yuki (why do they have British accents btw?) would have the saki bottle for example and fat sam would have the trap. Or, of course, old sniper man could also have the bottle.

Voice lines also tend to just pop up and repeat out of nowhere.

All in all — Just get Desperados III instead.

As usual. I'll start my review with TL;DR: Playing Shadow Tactics: Blade of the Shogun (ST for short) is like playing Mahjong Solitaire. In most levels there are a lot of guards between you and your objective. But you have to peel off the guards layer by layer or else you'll trigger an alarm. However, when playing ST you'll spend about 60~80% of your time just wresting with the control. Considering this game was released in 2016, [b]personally, I wouldn't spend more than 20 dollars on it. 25 tops[/b]. But if money ain't too tight, the art is indeed pretty good. It's just the control that's atrocious. Now I'll get in depth a little.

pros:
[list]
    [*]The core mechanics is kind of solid. Stealth and strategy was implemented in a really fun way. There are various NPC that have different types of behavior. And you have various characters each have their own unique flavor of abilities. creating various challenges where you have to figure out how to outsmart the enemy to achieve your goal.
    [*]Japanese voice acting created a really atmospheric environment. (provided that you choose the Japanese audio option, with English subtitles for those who don't speak Japanese)
    [*]The art is really flavorful. Both the graphics and the soundtracks are superb. Easily one of the top 10 I've seen in a decade.
    [*]Various in game challenges add a lot of replay value for those completionist.
    [*]The game features a quicksave and quickload system, one of the game's saving grace. The other being the art.
[/list]
cons:
[list]
    [*]There are a lot of in game dialogues and cutscenes which took place while the game is still in progress. Which makes it a lot harder to follow while you're trying to focus on playing the game. And that's one of my major complaints that loses the game some major point on the story department.
    [*]The game features a perspective camera at a 45° angle. While 45° angle camera shows off the game's many beautiful scenery, it's a poor choice for a tactical games. In some situation you'll end up with multiple transition or action point at the same area, and if you're so much as miss click by one pixel when issuing a command, all of a sudden your unit will charge up the hill and ended your game.
    [*]Lacks of proper pathing AI. This compounded on top of the previous camera problem. The game features a transition method where as if you want to move your character to the roof, up the ladder, into river, etc then you have to click on the transition point then the character will go interact with that transition point and transfer onto the new area. The problem is you'll have to basically hold your character's hand the entire time from one transition point to the next all the way to the next safe area. Which felt like you're babysitting your character and could get really tedious.
    [*]Enemy AI is sporadic at times. Certain NPC will for no reason go off script and does something it's not suppose to do. Even friendly NPC like Kuma will suddenly behave differently or crash entirely. Which happened to me once and I have to reload the last check point to fix it. Quite frankly speaking, without a quicksave/quickload system, this game would be completely unplayable.
    [*]The game lacks dedicated pause button. Which for a strategy game like this one is kind of a must have. There is a shadow mode that was executed weirdly in which you can [b]hold[/b] a command per character and tell them to execute simultaneously. However, it in practice when you have to enter shadow mode and issue a command, it is awkward that you need to enter shadow mode again to issue another command; what it should have done instead is to program it so that when you enter shadow mode you can issue multiple commands to multiple character sequentially and then exit shadow mode to execute simultaneously. On top of that, shadow mode doesn't freeze enemy in place so when you've finished setting the command the enemy NPC may not be in position for the command to function properly.
    [*]The game lacks a command queue to show what command it has registered. Again, something that would have worked really well for a strategy game like this one is the command queue which makes it that much clearer whether or not a command has been accepted. i.e: if I tell character A to do this to NPC X. Pause the game and show that in a queue so that I know that command has been accepted. Then I can move on to character B and figure out what to do with it.
    [*]The game imposes arbitrary and nonsensical restrictions on player to lengthen game time. Just to be clear, these restriction does not make the game harder or challenging, it's just makes more time consuming and tedious. One of the weird restriction is that Mugen can't not drop a body downwards. This is more prominent to me during mission 9 when one of the challenge requires you to hide all the bodies and you'll want to use Mugen as much as you can for it because he is the fastest character when carrying bodies and he can carry two instead of 1 for your three ninja unit.

    And then there's some weird AI detection restriction. In ST one of your ninja unit can disguise herself to fool the enemy, on the other hand there is also a unit that can see through the disguises so challenge you to path around the detector enemy. However, some of the later level features a snowy scene and character walking over snow will leave some footprints for a few seconds. What puzzles me is that the detector can somehow differentiates between friendly AI's footprints and your footprints, a setting which adds some arbitrary challenges that also makes no sense whatsoever.

   The most annoying of which involves the controllable raccoon Kuma. You can control a pet raccooon via another character. The weird thing is they impose a range restriction so that you can not placed Kuma too far from the raccoon owner. This is such a meaningless restriction that I'm sure on paper sounds like it adds more challenges but in reality, for me it only makes controlling Kuma more tedious. Because I figured out that you can interrupt Kuma when it moves by issuing a distract command. So late game I have to constantly move the character into position to move Kuma, then move the character back to stay out of view, then slowly lure the enemy guards away from their post to clear them one small group at a time. Which really, really isn't challenging for me, it's just wasted a lot of my time.
    [*]Enemy AI does not remove corpse upon discovery nor do they stay alert after discovering dead bodies. These are some of the questionable enemy AI behavior that breaks this game as a stealth game. Personally, and I can't believe I'm saying this, I prefer Hitman 2's AI behavior in which enemy AI will remove bodies. And in ST, since the game spawn a team of guard when they go into alert, it's possible to have it keep spawning enemy AI which creates more dead bodies and creates unnecessary burden on your computer.
    [*]Some of the level design were questionable. Especially the later level where the game gives you sparse disposing location, not even into river or down a mountain for no reason. It sucks.
[/list]

If you're still reading at this point, let me end with this for the time being. [h1]Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun[/h1] is by no means a bad game. It's very cool to see more Commandos and Desperados style games and the Japanese shogun Edo-era style is excellent, great audio and so on. Even the story elements are pretty enjoyable. 

However I felt I kept beating levels more so by exploiting flawed level design and running towards 'mission triggers', than actually cleverly solving the 'puzzle' of how to deal best with enemies remaining undetected and figuring out which order of attacks is optimal. As such, this game is much less like say Commandos 2 than one would actually expect. I'm going to say that's the biggest missed opportunity here. Because basically a lot of the ingredients for a great game are there. Now it's just average. It's definitely a buy at sale for fans of the genre, however the game does have a few very big flaws I can't ignore. For one the characters all 'freeze' for a second when they are spotted, which means you can basically forget about a hit and run type strategy, wait for alarm to be lowered and continue. I don't know if it's a bug, but with the vision cones gradually changing to yellow and red, a player expects to still be able to make a move and not have characters pinned until there are inevitable shots and damage.
On top of that, all characters are total glass canons in terms of hitpoints, but without strong range attacks for the most part. If you're spotted by more than two soldiers, you're most likely going to die without any ability to run very far. Even worse, some characters can't do simple tasks like climing a ladder or swimming in water, whereas others of your party can. That type of nonsense kills experimentation in how to beat levels, let alone have multiple solutions really.

I found some characters annoyingly vulnerable without much of a stronger attack able to deal with multiple enemies. What good is the samurai guy when taking on 3 is basically never a smart thing, when you have areas with 5 enemies almost constantly within 'alarm' distances, not to mention patrols that would return within 10s or so. This means that even with two characters and the 'planned moves' mode, you could only ever expect to take out a maximum of 4 enemies simultaneously. Especially in later levels this becomes very annoying and mostly a matter of quicksaving and reloading like there is no tomorrow just to inch forward in a level using just one character. I'm now 5 hours into this, a little more and it is starting to really get on my nerves. 

It's sadly not a very good stealth game when it comes to attacks. It lacks ranged attacks (yes, you sometimes have a sniper and sometimes a shuriken or trap, but you do not have those with every character and you don't get to pick your characters for each mission or something.) I kind of wish we have the ability to pick a character load-out, so we get access to traps and such in more than just that one character. It's weird the game doesn't ever really feel like true stealth gameplay is an option, but at the same time completely penalises any actions out in the open. That's basically the only reason why I can't recommend the game. As much as I would have loved to say otherwise, this game is not on par with the great Commandos games of old in how it plays out. I have to politely disagree with quicksave / quickloading as if it were a game mechanic. The Commandos games don't rely upon quicksaving for it's stealth gameplay to work well at all. Not recommending the game might sound a bit harsh, but as said fans of the genre might still like this having been basically starved of Commandos-like games. Just consider yourself warned it's not quite like that old game series.

[list]
[*] There is no inventory management. Your ninja guy can throw shurikens? Great, but he has only one and you have to collect it after every kill. Same goes for traps, bottles of beverage and so on.
[*] There is no other controllable characters than your 5 heroes (and you usually control only 2 or 3 in the mission). Unlike in Commandos 2 and 3 where you could sometimes control even 10 extra soldiers that you could loose, here you have only your heroes who cannot die and that's it.

[*] The game is too much puzzle-like. You spend hours watching enemy patrols and field of view and then retry multiple times, because if any enemy soldier sees you they will call reinforcements who will replace majority of the guards you killed. There is no place for mistakes - if you make one, you just have to load the previous save, because you won't be able to recover from that.

I don't have a ton to say on this one. I can fill a review page after just half an hour with some games, but here, I don't have a lot of complaints [i]or[/i] compliments. I'll get the latter out of the way first: the music is nice, the graphics are pleasant, the sound is good, and the user interface shows things off pretty well.

As for complaints, it largely comes to personal preference, I think. I will state, however, that I am a big fan of stealth in games, so this definitely falls in the realm of something that interested me, as opposed to me reviewing a football game or something else I was "fated" to dislike, almost guaranteed. One minor complaint is that I didn't feel like the controls were terribly intuitive, but the on-screen prompts addressed that well enough that it wasn't a deal-breaker for me.

What did turn me off completely, however, is that the game felt - to me - more like a puzzle game dressed as a stealth game than anything else, and while I like puzzles, constant trial-and-error start/restart quickloads on killing various enemies in an area until you kill the one or two enemies whose deaths won't alert everyone else in the area...it just really put me off. 

For instance, one mission has you hopping on top of carts and cliffs to avoid detection, but you need to kill specific guards, and to get to them, you have to take out every guard who can see them, or at least distract them long enough to kill and hide the body. There is a stream with guards and civilians across it who have pretty good vision distance, and it becomes a game of finding the one or two people who can't be seen to take them out, before moving along, taking out person after person until you're done. Also, killing civilians can lead to fail states, so this complicates matters.

Technically, I suppose that to some extent this falls under the category of I'm a wuss and I found it too difficult. However, [i]could[/i] I beat it? Sure! It's stealth, so with enough quicksaves, quickloads, and patience, eventually I would overcome the enemies. It would just take me a long time. Am I going to bother continuing, however? No, because I was never having fun while playing this game at any point. I am not playing it for the enjoyment of others, so if I'm having a bad time even after several hours, it would be a terrible idea for me to press on. At this point, cutting my financial losses and moving on to try to find another game that can make me happy is my best course of action.

Until you realise you can actually walk like 5m in front of guys looking straight at you and they have no idea you are there, then you might try all kinds of things. Once you realise you literally walk straight in front of people then the game gets a lot easier. Once you realise you can execute people with loud killing moves (slashes, screams, gurgles, slumps) right next to a guy looking the other way and he'll never know... it just makes no sense the way the gameplay is designed.

I really, really want to love this game.  The mechanics and design are wonderful, the Japanese voice acting is great, the Edo period is always a fun one to run around in, and it feels like Commandos: Sengoku Jidai Edition.

The problem is that the camera is often the worst and most persistent enemy in the game, camera controls are bound exclusively to the mouse (because there are too many keybinds for everything else to bind the camera to something responsive like WASD), and the biggest issue?  Lack of a pause function.

There is a "shadow mode" function that lets you issue an order to multiple units to execute them all simultaneously but in practice I found it to be virtually useless because it doesn't pause or even slow down time, and it was very rare that I had multiple units that would complete their task (typically killing or otherwise incapacitating a guard) at the same time because different units move at different speeds and have different animations (Yuki takes much longer to kill someone than does Mugen, for example, and Aiko moves much faster than Hanzo.)

There's also the potential problem that this is basically Save Scum: The Game.  The devs have explicitly said that save scumming is part of the intended design... yet have also said that they didn't put a pause function into the game because it wouldn't fit the deisgn... presumably because it would break the flow or feeling of the game?  So pausing the game to issue a single command to your dudes breaks the flow of the game, while quickloading literally every 5-10 seconds doesn't?  I mean... if they say so, I guess.

There's also the issue of the game having guards and NPCs with Skyrim levels of stupidity and obliviousness, and NPCs rigorously do the same thing in an infinite, unchanging loop.  They do not react to the world around them in an even remotely believable way - a rock randomly falls on someone and after an exclamation of "I noticed that!" and about 30 seconds of "search mode" behavior, they return to what they were doing before... even if the rock just fell on someone that, as far as the mission narrative is concerned, is an important person and not some bottom-level mook.

The game HAS to be this way because the developers apparently refused to try putting in a pause function or anything like it that would allow for more tactical complexity and more detailed AI behavior.  Because it might take you thirty tries to execute a plan (because you have to issue the commands in real time and wrangle with the camera the whole way through), everything needs to be in a constant state of stasis - guards patrol the exact same paths (which are typically just a simple loop, nothing complex, and never a series of different loops or paths), civilians pick up the same pile of wood and bring it to the same location at which point it vanishes and they go retrieve another identical pile of wood, an important NPC you need to steal documents from always goes and prays at the same shrine by himself for the same amount of time at the exact same time interval even as you're gradually picking off his guards and dumping their corpses in the bushes one by one every time he leaves the immediate area.

I really do want to love this game.  It's clear a lot of work went into it and the production values are absolutely fantastic.  But it's hamstrung by the developers making a staggeringly stupid decision to not allow any sort of slow-mo or pause function into the game.  By refusing to go down that path, they're forced to dumb down the rest of the game to compensate and as a result the entire thing is badly limited.  I cannot recommend this game because of that.

RTS Stealth games are a rare breed, and this game is probably unlike most in the stealth genre in that you command a whole party with unique skill sets. The individual characters are fairly pedestrian—a traditional ninja that relies on mid-range shuriken and misdirection, a warrior with an emphasis on combat but weak stealth, a low mobility sniper, a trap master, and a disguise character that can move in-and-out of enemy lines undetected. That being said, the game stands out by giving players access to all of them (with your roster shifting from mission-to-mission), and treating each character as a set of interesting tools to solve your mission objectives.

Unfortunately, Shadow Tactics is also at war with its camera and has some frustrating design elements that sour the overall experience: 

1) Shadow Tactics is the type of games that demands absolute precision and timing from its players, but you only have limited control over the camera and some actions are only possible from specific camera angles. It's the absolute worst when you're about to execute a daring manuever or take out a guard, but you realize at the last second that you have the wrong camera angle and less than a second to find the correct one before a guard raises the alarm. I have no issue with stealth games being challenging, but it ruins the whole experience when you have to reload for the umpteenth time because terrible camera controls rather than a misplay. 

2) Shadow Tactics is horrid at communicating basic information to players. The basic game play loop revolving around abusing gaps in guard patrols and vision cones, but vision cones indicated in subtle shades of green that often blur into the surrounding color palette. If you are color blind, have vision problems of any kind, or even just use the wrong type of lighting around your computer monitor, players risk missing out on key information and be forced to reload for the umpteenth time.

3) Most importantly, Shadow Tactics is a game built around quick save abuse. The margin of error in Shadow Tactics is functionally non-existent, so players are encouraged to quick save frequently and reload whenever they make a mistake. In small doses, this is a lovely feature, but reloading dozens or even hundreds of times per mission will be common for most players (at least on their first playthroughs). After awhile, the game starts to feel less like a set of an exciting infiltrations, assassinations, and heists, and more like filling forms in triplicate after you reload for the umpteenth time because the camera bugged out at the last moment (and god help you if you haven't quick saved recently). 

I wanted to like Shadow Tactics. I really did. Still, that isn't an excuse for the critical lack of polish and terrible design decisions. If you can look past all of its awkward game mechanics, the camera that seems set up to fail, and tweak the graphics to avoid missing out on key information, you'll have a wonderful time with this rare gem. However, I can't recommend this game in good conscience to anyone but the most diehard stealth fans that can overlook its many, many flaws.

[b][u]General Thoughts/Overview:[/u][/b]

Shadow Tactics: Blades of the shogun (ST) is a commando clone done right. It strips the concept right back to its fundamentals, and does a damned good job of providing a mechanically sound game. You oversee a team of characters engaging in asymmetric warfare. Small numbers means intelligent play, requiring you to sneak, stab, trap, distract, and lure guards as you penetrate deeper towards your goal. The characters themselves have diverse skills and tool sets, filling different roles which allow for multiple methods of approach as you disassemble the Rube Goldberg machine of guards to get to the juicy mission complete screen. 

[b][u]Pros:[/u][/b]
[list][*] Mechanically this game is spot on. Different types of guard, multiple approaches, diverse skills, varied levels with multiple mechanics, ST is an excellent example of how to make a tactical stealth game both challenging and well thought out.  
[*] The story is passable. Mostly predictable, but executed, voice acted, and played out very well. 
[*] The artwork, ambient audio, level design, interactions, and surrounding theme and ‘feel’ of the game are also spectacular. 
[/list]

[b][u]Cons:[/u][/b]
[list][*] The missions are long winded, to the point where some feel bloated for what they are.
[*] The game can be EXTREMELY frustrating. There are seemingly endless numbers of occasions where kills are seen by guards you didn’t see, or on the cusp of someone you saw but didn’t think was in range’s vision. It makes the disassembly of the machine lack a lot of the satisfaction it could get if it wasn’t built in a way which often feels unfair. (It makes sense, though, from a theme stand point.)
[*] The game hides the medals and award objectives first play through. This is frustrating as it is simply baiting multiple play-through’s the levels just don’t warrant. 
[/list]

[b][u]Suggested improvements:[/u][/b]
 [list][*] Tokens to be used to buy upgrades. Small things like ‘show bodies on map’ and unlocking skill based challenges could have been rewards which would fit the theme without deducting from the experience or altering the difficulty. 
[*] More enemy types/environment types and interactions between the characters.
[*] Maybe it’s already present, but I’d have enjoyed Japanese audio subtitled in English, and couldn’t see a way to make that happen.  
[/list]


[b][u]Overall Recommendation:[/u][/b]

The thing is, while this game did [i]everything[/i] right mechanically, it just wasn’t [i][b]fun[/b][/i], and that, is a real problem. I appreciate this game, I liked the challenge, and I felt the story, audio, art, and setting were fantastic. But at no point did I feel like I could say “Yeah, this is really fun, and I’m really enjoying this”. In fact, I frequently breathed a sigh of relief after I beat a level, [i]because it meant that it was over.[/i] The only thing that kept me playing was the fact it was so challenging in the right way.

This game is not for impatient people. It is isn’t for people who want fast paced nonstop action, and it isn’t for people who are easily frustrated. 

This game is for people seeking a challenge. It is for people who enjoy tactical stealth, people who enjoy systematic disassembly of things, and for people who want an immersive game about heroes set in medieval Japan. 

Ultimately, for me, I want to enjoy my games as well as appreciate them, so it's an overall no from me. But that said, this very much might be for you.

There are positives, like the pretty environments and lively art direction, but because of a combination of frustrating elements, the game becomes a frustrating grind that discourages tactical thinking and has you fighting the controls and save scumming constantly.

The maps are large, and the missions typically take an hour or two to beat, but there's no way to see the whole map at once. The zoom is woefully limited, meaning that planning a route through from the start to the goal is impossible. You find yourself taking on every little area one at a time, unable to plan for what's next, and looking back and realizing it would have been faster to go another way. Every guard is watched by at least one other guard. Killing guards becomes a process of tediously killing your way through an entire section of the map just so you can kill one guard that was blocking a gate.

For a stealth tactics game, the maps are also shockingly linear. Sure, it's open, but there's only one path that doesn't lead to certain death. After a time, you get the impression that every map has one main designed path with a few shortcuts, and every area, every section of the map is just a puzzle to solve (and time correctly). I didn't once feel like I could experiment with using different combinations of abilities, or one mission, going vertical, or going sneaking on another. I can't count the number of times I thought "Oh, I'd have loved to have this character right now, I wonder how I could use his explosive with her powder.." etc. except that every mission has a specific loadout of characters. I never felt like I had a creative choice in my use of abilities or characters. And even with the characters you get, working together is pointless. Even the abilities each character has seems unnecessarily limited. Only one character can throw rocks? Only one character can make a luring noise? It's arbitrary decisions like this that make the gameplay uncreative.

The squad mechanics are almost non-existent. I found myself playing most of the maps one character at a time, only changing when I faced a situation that required a different character's abilities. You can only control one character at a time, except to move, and even then it's a disaster because they all have different movement speeds and collide with each other constantly, frequently catching the guards' attention. The only way to use your characters together is using "shadow mode" which allows you to queue actions from different characters so you can execute them at once. HOWEVER, shadow mode only allows you to queue up ONE ACTION per character, making complex planning (i.e. shadow TACTICS) virtually excluded by design. The game wants you to control characters and make decisions in real-time, but making real-time decisions is impossible because the maps are crawling with guards, and this is [i] not a combat game. [/i] If you're spotted by a guard, game over is all but certain. Reinforcements begin to shoot from afar, you cannot fight more than one guard, you cannot run, you cannot become invisible. Even if you do manage to escape, the entire map will be on alert, making the rest of the mission nearly impossible. And your other characters CANNOT HELP AT ALL because again, REAL TIME. If you're spotted, your sniper can't take out the guard, your heavy can't clear the guards, because without that action-planning, by the time you switch to them, it's too late. The game becomes about timing, waiting and save-scumming over and over to get characters across the map, one by one.

That brings me to the save-scumming. It's included in the gameplay by design, even going as far as to include a timer reminding you to constantly save. Some others don't mind this, but I personally found it frustrating and flow-breaking. The game relies on save-scumming because it's the only way the player can time moves perfectly enough to succeed because the stealth, squad teamwork, and combat mechanics are not effective enough alone because they can't be properly planned and executed. It makes the gameplay tedious, and when it collides with the controls, it becomes truly frustrating.

The majority of the game relies on the mouse, and a few clunky hotkeys. Switching between characters takes too long to perform actions across characters in real-time. Executing actions, however, is the true nail in the coffin. I can't count the number of times I've clicked on a guard to kill them, and instead, without my realizing, the kill skill wasn't toggled, and my character walks right up to the guard and sits there, waiting for death. Me too, buddy. Or that I thought I clicked on the ground but instead clicked on a wall, and then my character walks out in front of a guard, reload the save. Or, that I had the wrong character selected, and again, ruined the play. The camera is not suitable for the amount of tight spaces and vertical elements in the game. You can't look top down, and rotating the camera requires stopping whatever else you're doing.

Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun is a faithful continuation of the near-dead genre of squad-based tactics games. As others have said, it is most similar to the 90s-era game series Commandos. You control a squad that grows to 5 unique characters, each with their own abilities that you must use together to overcome the enemies ahead of you.

If you're familiar with and enjoyed Commandos -- or any other top-down squad tactics game -- then you would probably enjoy this game. That is, you'd at least enjoy the type of gameplay it's trying to re-create. However, as of writing this on the 3rd level, I've come across too many mission-ending bugs that make this game much more frustrating than enjoyable to play. These bugs get in the way of playing the game way too often.

As others have said in negative reviews, I was pressing F5 and F8 to quick-save and -load the game so often it was becoming tedious. But, unlike the other reviews, I wasn't pressing F5 and F8 because I was testing tactics to see what stuck; after doing that a couple of times, you get an idea of the usability of the characters' skills enough to know what to do with them. The game also has a pretty linear formula, where each part of a mission has one or two solutions that the game is waiting for you to figure out: there's one order to kill the 5 guards in so they don't see, or you can walk over the house roofs and avoid the conflict. But that is what these kind of games are about, with having a planned solution kind of waiting to be discovered.

However, even when you figure it out, the aforementioned bugs come into play. For example, there's a 100% reproducible bug in that if you move a unit and then queue up more moves for them, the first queued move will be skipped. This lead to me failing a mission a handful of times because I would give a unit orders, then leave to give another orders, and he would walk into a guard's view instead of outside the view range. There is also a problem with the isometric camera, in that sometimes you'll click to have a unit hide in a bush beyond a wall but the click will register on the wall, so they will begin moving around the wrong way. There are also the times when you'lll click the edge of the roof to prep a ninja for a drop-attack, only to have them vapidly jump to the ground next to the target guard instead. There are also occurences of guards seeing crouched characters behind cover, when I did the very same thing next quickload and they were undetected. Sometimes guards on the snow level I quit on will see snowy footprints on cleared paths and through bushes.

Anyway, the reason I put this game down is that I was doing a part of a mission where you have to distract a group of guards and then pickpocket an item from a civilian. I would keep doing the same run, but had to repetitively load because one or another of these bugs would happen, sometimes sooner into the strategy and sometimes near the end. So, I found my self quicksaving in smaller and smaller increments, anticipating one of the bugs ruining my tactic and getting more and more frustrated before giving up. I had spent 20 minutes throwing myself at the same situation over and over again, and the lack of Quality Control had ended up beating me, not a lack of strategy.

If they fix the bugs with queued and synced actions, the AI issues, and make the UI click-through and camera problems, this game is definitely worth it. As it is, it's still quite playable, but you'll have the flow of gameplay broken up with infuriating bugs that require you to keep hitting rewind.

The game is decent, but it grapples with a well-known issue that many have pointed out—the challenge of precise timing. While executing actions with precise timing is typical in RTS games like this, Shadow Tactics takes it up a notch, especially with the abundance of dense enemy situations. There are instances where you might find yourself waiting for the perfect moment to carry out your planned action, sometimes for dozens of minutes. Rushing through can lead to unfortunate consequences. 

In conclusion, the game has its merits, but it may not be everyone's cup of tea. So, proceed with caution.

I'm honestly shocked to see this game rated as "overwhelmingly positive." I would say that for me, this one was a miserable slog. The story is token, but fine. Real trope-y. But, it's got a neat Kurosawa vibe that I really dig. It's fun enough. For me, 
though, the choices the devs made for the interface and gameplay loop are absolutely baffling. This is one of the few games I've ever played that I've disliked so much that I've decided to push through and beat it purely out of spite for the mechanics of it.

First off, it's marketed as a strategy game, but it is only a strategy game in the loosest sense. This is a puzzle game wrapped in an RTS interface. In a strategy game, as "strategy" is marketed in gaming, you plan your moves and react to the moves your opponent planned. In a puzzle game, you manipulate the environment and the actors in the environment to progress the game. In this game, you move several characters through what is basically a series of obstacle courses with a ninja theme. You need to use the tools your characters have to kill NPCs and manipulate the environment to get to the finish line. To me, this is no different from doing a sudoku puzzle; I would contrast this with, say, playing a game of chess or checkers or Total War: Shogun 2. There is nothing dynamic about your actions in this game: you are presented with a map full of NPCs and environmental cues, and if you to look hard enough at the clues and move your characters with just the right timing, eventually you'll beat the level. Is this necessarily bad? No. Not necessarily. I was disappointed that this isn't really an RTS or turn-based strategy game, but I was totally open to a puzzle game framed in a ninja obstacle course. And is there a strategy to puzzles? Yeah, sometimes. So is it pedantic for me to criticize this game for being a puzzle rather than a dynamic strategy game? Maybe. A puzzle game /can/ have strategic elements. But, the problem is, whether you call this game a ninja strategy game or a ninja puzzle game, Mimimi throws it all out the window with the gameplay loop. 

In my eyes, a strategy game has to have a gameplay loop that involves some combination of planning, action, reaction, and consequences. This game has a gameplay loop that involves "attempting" and "succeeding or reloading." There is no "react" option in this game. There is no planning for failures or reacting to failures. There is no "plan b." Why? Because you have unlimited quicksaves that you can use at any time, making this, essentially, 'save-scum' the game. If you plan poorly and get your characters killed, you have a reset button with unlimited uses. The devs did make mechanics for your characters getting "spotted" and alarms going off, but you will likely see this in-game once or twice at most, because you will quickload the second things go wrong. The second you get spotted, you'll time-warp back to before you got spotted, and adjust your "strategy" to accommodate whatever minute and obscure environmental factor it was that you didn't catch before. Any time you make any elaborate action with any character, you will be quicksaving at every mouse-click and loading the second it goes wrong. This is enforced by the fact that your game ends when any one character dies, and any character dies within two seconds of alerting the level's guards. 

It's... baffling to me why the devs would set up a decent game, great atmosphere, fun characters and character interactions (combining character skills is where the game shines), and then throw it all out the window by making save-scumming the core gameplay loop. If they had balanced their game's mechanics and fine-tuned the clunky interface, rather than promoting cheesing the gameplay, they could have had something really great. I'll point out that they include a slew of incredibly intricate achievements that you really would have to attack the puzzles with a strategic mindset to complete. "Beat the level without killing a guard" sort of things. But, the quicksaving is still a part of these achievements. Maybe if you play to nab all of these achievements, the game could be a challenging, strategic puzzle experience. But for myself, and, if achievement statistics are to be believed, most players, who beat every level pretty easily but are still frustrated with the clunky UI and still cheesing the character synergies to the extreme, it's a pretty mediocre experience.

If I had to sum it up, I'd say this game is the equivalent of doing a sudoku puzzle with a pencil rather than a pen. Fuck up? No worries- this ain't going on your permanent record. Just erase it and go back and look a little harder.

I can only recommend this game if you are experienced with, and enjoy this style of game. Otherwise I wouldn't recommend it. I'm aware of the overwhelmingly positive reviews, hear me out.

I usually play traditional  RPGs, tactical battlers, some action shooters, and ARPGs. I bought this game because I love feudal Japan period and I have fond memories of Commandos. I gave it a shot, it's not for me.  Here's why I wouldn't recommend it to anyone other than lovers of this genre:

1.  This is barely 'tactics'. Yes when you have more than 2 characters on the map there is some tactics but otherwise there's a lot of restiction of what can actually be done. 
2. It's very linear. despite the large playmaps, they mostly have 1 or 2 set paths/formulas to solve them. There's a few environmental type traps dotted around to interact with but not a lot. The outside maps have slightly more 'open world' but the villages/building rich maps mostly have a path to follow (roof hooks, jumpable roofs etc).
3. The skill in this game is pattern memorization and timing. It's like playing an action platformer where you need to get your timing spot on. Basically memorize the guard patrols and time your moves between view cones. 
4. Very trial & error (I suppose most games are trial and error to some extent). It's a quickload spammer. And very frustrating in parts.
5. I would of liked control on who (which characters) to bring to each mission. Then we'd have a proper tactics game and proper  problem solving.

Otherwise:

1. Really loved the feudal Japan setting and theme.
2. Graphics are really nice.
3. Game runs well, no glitches or bugs that I came across.
4. Good selection of achievements, badges, awards, challenges etc that can be earned.

I can see it's a quality game and a lot of people are enjoying it, but I honestly can't receommend it to anyone but lovers of this particular genre.

Ordinarily I'd welcome these kind of challenges in my stealth games but why for the love of god are there speedrunning badges?! It goes against EVERYTHING this game is about: slow and methodical stealth, trial-and-error learning, taking in the setting and all the wonderful details that go along with it. Speedrunning's inclusion is just a symptom of a broader issue though, as it shows a shocking lack of thought from a team that seems otherwise quite capable of meticulously crafting a most unique and interesting gaming experience. Speedrunning I'd argue is a game in itself, and the skills and fun involves are often tailored to a very specific niche of players. By having me do speedrun in order to 100% the game, it all but squashed every bit of my desire to replay the game. And replay value is important for a level-driven stealth game like Shadow Tactics. And so the developers' misstep here is not just a minor one, it's serious enough to prevent me from wanting to recommend it to other players like myself.

(2) Clumsy controls: It's easy to be overwhelmed by the relief and the odd sense of accomplishment after you complete another gruelling level that takes forever and often makes you go "What the fuck is this and why do I subject myself to such torture?" To the point where you're almost willing to forget the countless times you get spotted and have to reload because of some bs not of your making (e.g., inconsistent detection, controlled character just standing behind guards like total idiots and refusing to kill them). Clumsy controls would've been more tolerable had the game been more forgiving but a lot of times these split-second moments of input-output disconnect mean the game CANNOT BE PLAYED AS INTENDED, i.e., as a highly precise, elegant, tactical stealth game where you're given all the tools and the options to figure out challenging but fair scenarios. Clumsy control, by taking away the fairness, left me often feeling quite empty after completing a level because I could only have done so because of circumstantial exploits. It's not Sekiro where you "git gud". Rather you just keep trying until you suddenly manage to "squeeze through a tight crack" without knowing if that's what you're "supposed to do". I like doing logical proofs so it's not the case that the "puzzle aspect" of the game inhibits player expression and I think this kind of approach to gameplay is dead by default. I fully acknowledge that this is not Assassin's Creed or Hitman where the game is equal part action as it is stealth. There is often times only one way to complete the missions and part of the fun is just figuring out what that may be. Whilst I think I'd enjoy a game like this (admittedly Shadow Tactics could at times be extremely fun precisely because it gleefully hints at but never quite manages to live up to its potential), the controls (even on PC, god-forbid I ever try playing this again but with a controller!) made me feel like half the battle was just with the inconsistent outputs themselves.

(3) Limited dynamicism: I think having a logic-like structure to "solving" stealth encounters and being dynamic are not mutually exclusive. There just needs to be more mechanics, more dynamic events and a greater variety of NPC states. Sadly the only interesting mechanic approaching something like this is a "Shadow Mode" where you get to control the actions of all your party members at once. But you can't chain these or create synergy. It's just a one-time move that you execute only to have to clumsily clean up its effects by individually controlling each character again, making the mechanic another one of the game's underdeveloped ideas that could've been so much more (not to mention an annoying bug where characters would refuse to do a high-profile kill no matter how many times you double-click in Shadow Mode). The late-game levels are so challenging that using Shadow Mode becomes a must and so these flaws only become more glaring with the game's heavy emphasis on the mechanic. I don't think Shadow Tactics has to necessarily give up its real-time gameplay but if the developers are willing to sacrifice urgency by blatantly encouraging save-scumming, then that means the real-time gameplay isn't really there to promote urgency but to promote dynamicism. If so where's the dynamicism? NPC behaviour is often times so basic (consisting of a grand total of three states: neutral, alerted and in conflict) that one can't help but default to the "baseline strategy" of maximising the first, using the second to maximise the first and minimising the last. This realistically translates into a "kill my way across the map" because it's just objectively the easiest way to progress. And since nobody likes to get stuck I suspect most people's first playthrough looked quite similar too, which all makes for a very drab and monotone experience. Unless somehow after all this one is still interested in another playthrough (I certainly am not) this means the game for most people is just one strategy throughout, for something that supposedly promotes active strategic engagement.

Like I said I think it's a good game at heart and a very commendable effort at revitalising the top-down tactical stealth genre. And whilst I at times had a lot of fun with the game, ultimately the lows of the game were unfortunately much much lower than its highs. It's sad to think that Mimimi won't be making any more games like this because I honestly think given experience and time the formula could be refined to result in something truly amazing. But as it stands, Shadow Tactics is laboured, exhausting and blundering. Looking back at the 44 hours I spent there was more me looking at the map dreading having to do the same shit and suffer through the same bs again than genuine moments of surprise or epiphany for succeeding.

Blade of the Shogun starts out  fantastic. Isometric stealth game play that requires planning and precision. It's incredibly difficult, but the game gives you the ability to save at any point which stops it from being too frustrating. 

Despite all this praise, the game quickly runs thin in terms of game play and quality. As the difficulty increases from hard to harder, the auto save feature becomes a crutch, not to prevent mistakes, but to repeatedly try precise and complicated movements kills. The strategic elements get thinner too as the player relies more and more on cheesier attempts to knock out loners and pull people away from the group. It becomes a pretty stale rhythm. Each level has a unique gimmick to play around, but it only represents a small part of the stage and the rest of the time you are back to the same strategies you use in every stage. 

Outside of the strategic side, the increase in difficulty and precision quickly creates annoyances with the technical elements of the game. Npcs will spaz out on occasion, your characters won't follow your orders quite right, and the camera becomes so cumbersome. The camera controls in this game are AWEFUL. 

The camera lets you switch between four viewpoints, each from one of the four diagonals. But why. Why can't I place the camera wherever I want. Also, your movements can be restricted by the camera because you only have four angles. Certain camera angles will block the space you want to click. Case in point, I had an instance where I couldn't physically click a perfectly legal location because it was blocked by the camera rotations.

Overall, I really do think its a decent enough game, if not enough variety on the strategy overall. But it quickly gets bogged down by an issue most games that require precision and perfection from the player: the game itself doesn't offer the tools to accomplish the needed levels of control. You can't require me to be 100% precise and the controls only offer 90% control. Every time it happens just builds frustration. 

Finally, and most aggresiously overall are the bonus goals. It won't affect most people but holy crap are they poorly thought out and implemented. You have a list of bonus objectives and challenges for 100% completion, and the way they have been implemented is borderline offensive. You have 9 goals and objectives, and it doesn't tell you on your first go around, for no reason I can see. Added to this, many objectives may be exclusive and can't be accomplished in the same try as the others. This means you may very well have to play the same stage five times in addition to the starting clear. Why? Why would you make it like that? Unknowning what this game had to offer I purchased it with no real expectations until after my experience. After spending some time with it Shadow Tactics this was a great concept for a genre not seen often nowadays, but poorly executed where game mechanics are concerned.

The positives however is despite this being a stealth based game, the developers did take great care is keeping historically with the time setting, Edo period Japan, and also crafting a very enjoyable story. Watch the cutscenes and listinging to the in game dialogues amongst the characters was enjoyable. In addition the 5 playable chacters were all given personalities that again made their interactions with one another enjoyable. For a top down game the graphics were not bad, almost appearing in a style similar to a Warcraft or Diablo feel. In addition several of the cutscenes were nicely designed. 

Though as to the negatives there are many. First is the horrid camera system. Taking a top down approach, the player is forced to constantly rotate the cameras by function of two keys swinging it left to right. Though there is a free moment aspect where you could see in some freeform aspect there is no true free camera mechanic to see all areas of the level. This makes it extremely frustrating in that you are unable to see all areas of the level, even with using the zoom feature of the camera system to widen or narrow the view. 

Secondly is the spotting system. The game employees a spotting mechanic where enemies have a field of vision that determines whether you are spotted are not. Some ranges, indicated by the solid color fill of the field of vision clearly indicate what they can see where as  a spotted pattern indicates where you can be in front of them but remain hidden so long as you are in stealth mode aka crouching. However I had experience many times where the characters I am positioning within the spotted zone are registered as being seen even though they are in stealth mode. In addition the field of vision for enemies can be blocked by large items which is part of the strategy of this game though I have found this to to be very buggy. In many cases I had the characters position behind such objects where the field of vision is shown as clearly blocked yet somehow the games still registers the character as being seen.

Thirdly is the slow down mechanics. Part of the field of vision, when an enemy spots a character the field of vision turns red indicating that you have been spotted. However, when spotted the character is automatically rendered to move very slowly. So slow in fact running away becomes useless as the enemies vision registry, indicated by the growing of the red color, catches up to you faster than you can run away. It is at this point you pretty much have to reload the game as running away or fighting the enemies that have spotted you becomes useless. Yes even running to kill them is not an option as you are slowed and they will kill you before you have a chance to reach them.

Fourthly is the prolong kill animations. Taking out the enemies is an option but almost again useless as the animations are so long it isn't worth it as you are more than likely going to be spotted for doing it. For instance, one of the characters weilds a knife and the kill animation is a three strike combo. It is evident that this was done for more of a stylish look but   
in a stealth game where seconds matter it is useless and unnecessary. Several other kill options such as using a gun, setting traps, and many others have the same situation.

Fifthly is the clicking registry system. For some enviromental interaction the game registers one eviromental action despite you wanting something else. A clear example of this are for the characters who can use grappling hooks. When attempting to simply move them close to an area, such as the base of a wall, rather than register your mouse click as movement action and displaying the destination icon to indicate where you are moving to, the game instead renders you as wanting to use the character's grappling hook by quickly changing the icon to that action. The only remedy to this is changing the camera angle where you have a much better chance of getting the desired effect you want. This was but one of many instances I have observed where the game registers you actions as something else. 

 Besides flawed game mechanics, the developers also made a poor choice in the voice acting department when listing in English. Several of the actors were native English speakers attempting horrible Japanese accents. It was so bloody bad my ears cringed. Luckily there is an option to change the voice setting to Japanese that was more pleasent to listen to. 

In all this game did have the potential but with the flawed mechanics it was not something I enjoyed playing. I cannot say I would recommend this.

[h3][b][u]Short Answer:[/u][/b][/h3] A stealth game with a lot of good ideas, but also a frustrating progression curve that changes the gameplay for the worse. The five characters you control are well-balanced and fun to use, and the first half of the game provides a steady stream of interesting mechanics while offering you the ability to tackle every challenge in several different ways. However, the second half of the game increases in difficulty in a way that severely limits your freedom, turning every encounter into a puzzle where only one correct solution exists. Sources of fun in its design became sources of frustration, and I ended up dropping it right before the finale.

[h3][b][u]Long Answer:[/u][/b][/h3] [i]Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun[/i] is marketed as a real-time strategy/stealth game set in the Edo period of Japan, where five individuals--specialists in skills like infiltration, espionage, and assassination--are recruited by the newly-appointed shogun to fight back against a conspiracy that threatens to end the nation's newfound peace. I say it's "marketed" as a real-time strategy/stealth game because even though it may start out this way, over time it manages to turn itself into something else--something that ultimately left me frustrated and disappointed, as it changed too much from what first piqued my interest.

The core gameplay is about what you'd expect: you need to use the wide range of tools at your disposal to sneak through a metaphorical minefield of enemies, accomplishing goals like gathering information or assassinating key figures in the rebellion against the shogun, getting in and out without anyone even realizing that you were there. There are five different characters, and each of the game's 13 missions will have you control between two and four of them depending on what the story calls for--only one mission has you using all five at the same time, but one of the five is kept on such a tight leash that you're effectively just playing with four. The playable characters are all very good, and each one is unique from one another in almost every way: what tools they have to distract and attack, how quickly their attacks can dispatch an enemy, and even their approach to moving a dead/unconscious body. Each one has their strengths and weaknesses, and by far the best part of the game is how well-balanced they are, since each one is able to tackle obstacles or otherwise fill a niche that the others can't. [b]Though many missions can have you prioritizing one character over the rest, they all feel like valuable parts of the team and will all get their chance to shine multiple times throughout your playthrough.[/b]

The first 7 missions ease you into all the mechanics the game has to offer, and [b]there are a lot of interesting mechanics on display here[/b]. Aside from the different character traits, you're introduced to different enemy types that are unaffected by some/most skills and require more careful planning to dispatch; as well as environmental changes that can make it easier or harder to stay hidden, like snow that leaves a footprint trail or nighttime missions that alter enemies' cones of vision. It can be hard to keep track of all of this when approaching a new obstacle--character traits especially, in my case--but it's very rewarding when you put it all together to come up with a solution. Every mission offers multiple solutions to reach the end goal, and you can even earn optional badges for completing missions in specific ways, so [b]you're given some freedom to decide how you want to tackle each challenge--or at least you are at first[/b]. Unfortunately, [b]missions start to feel more and more constrained as you progress[/b], and therein lies my main problem with [i]Shadow Tactics[/i].

No new major mechanics are added after mission 7, so missions 8-13 increase the difficulty mainly by increasing the enemy quantity/density, with a few new iterations on learned mechanics sprinkled in (e.g. a nighttime snow mission). This means an absurd amount of overlapping lines of sight for nearly every enemy and point of interest on the map, often with vision cones coming in from off-screen thanks to very limited map zoom, which greatly reduces the actions you can perform without a very poor outcome. Your goal is no longer to find the various ways you can infiltrate a new area, it's to parse out the single weakest link in a cluster of enemies, the single skill that's capable of dispatching that one enemy without getting caught, and the [i]very[/i] short window between multiple staggering patrols that will let you actually get to them; rinse and repeat. It [i]is[/i] still possible to beat every mission several different ways, as evidenced by the aforementioned badges; but the difference in difficulty between the "optimal" path and other paths grows so high that they no longer feel like reasonable options. The entire second half of my playthrough almost felt like I was playing a completely different game--[b]it stopped feeling like a strategy game with multiple paths to victory and started feeling like a puzzle game with only one "correct" solution.[/b] There's nothing inherently wrong with that kind of level design, but only when the player goes into it knowing to expect that. When the first half indulged the ability to think outside the box, the stifling feeling the second half created went against what got me hooked on the game in the first place.

This is a bit of a side tangent, but [b]the consequence for mistakes during a mission feels too high, even on the "Normal" difficulty setting meant for first-time players[/b]. If you or a body you left behind are spotted, it alerts nearby enemies [i]and[/i] spawns in additional ones that won't leave after things die down, instead taking up new permanent patrols nearby. This means that making even a small mistake can make the current section much harder for yourself, as well as derail any potential plans you might have had for getting to the next area. You're encouraged to make liberal use of the quicksave/quickload options while playing, so the answer to making mistakes isn't to find a clever way to recover--like creating a diversion so you can make a getaway--it's to just reload and try again. It deters you from making the kind of risky yet rewarding plays that can make stealth gameplay exhilarating, conditioning you instead to keep repeating the same brief segments over and over again in a further pursuit towards that singular "correct" solution I mentioned earlier. 

[b]I put over 20 hours into this game, making it all the way to the last mission before my frustration finally boiled over.[/b] The last few missions took most of what I found enjoyable about the game at the start of my playthrough and turned it into sources of aggravation by the end of it: time spent planning my moves kept growing until it became tedious, the use of certain characters at each obstacle felt like a required step I had to complete instead of a choice I got to make, and the branching paths on a map just made it harder to find the "right" path to a less exhausting victory. Normally I'd recommend giving the demo a try since that can give you a clearer idea of what to expect than a written review can; but seeing as it only takes you through the first level, I don't know that it'll properly convey the issues I've mentioned here. That being said, if what I've described sounds like something you can work around or doesn't sound like a problem at all, then I hope you have a better time with it than I did. [b][u][i]Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun[/i] started off promising, but in the end it turned into an experience that was much more frustrating than fun for me.[/u][/b]

Shadow Tactics is an RTS puzzle game that is a mixed bag of some enjoyment but a huge amount of frustration and terrible design.

You get 5 characters throughout the game and they essentially all work the same with the exception of the sniper.  They all have a close range blade attack, a special move only they can do, a different distraction/luring technique, a limited use flintlock, and a 1 time use medkit.  The sniper has limited ammo in his long range rifle as his main attack and a limited number of grenades as his special move.  Early on you only get a couple characters per mission but later on you'll get access to 4 or 5.  Unfortunately the balance isn't very good.  The 2 female characters make the male characters pretty much useless as Yuki's trap/whistle combo can take care of pretty much every regular enemy and once Aiko gets a disguise you'll run around with her killing every lone unit or distracting someone so someone else can kill the person he was watching.  The only time you'll need the male characters is to take out an enemy samurai.

So to get to the frustrations and terrible design.  The entire game is a giant grindy save scum.  You will be quick saving after pretty much every enemy you kill, every time you move to a new position, every time you get ready to set up a new kill, every time you hide a body somewhere, etc.  Then you'll constantly be quick loading as something goes wrong, whether you get screwed over by the god awful camera, whether your character does something completely random you didn't want them to do, you get spotted by some enemy 2 miles away, spotted by some guy who looks like he's looking in a completely different direction, or spotted by some dude who just happened to walk into view range as you started killing.  Anytime you're spotted you're going to press F8 since being spotted alarms enemies.  They swarm the area for a minute+ before they go back to their normal spots.  It's always quicker to quick load.  Fortunately the game quick saves and loads quickly.  I want to be entirely clear here.  I am not exaggerating in any way, shape or form.  On average, you will be quick saving or quick loading at least every 30 seconds.

The cursor and character actions are a gigantic problem.  The cursor will often completely miss what you're trying to do.  Did you tell your character to walk up and stab that guy?  Well instead the game interprets it as you having told your character to walk right in front of that enemy and stand there.  F8.  I don't even want to talk about dragging bodies because this p!ssed me off all game long.  Tell character to drag a body over to a bush and drop it.  Come back to that character later and they're standing in the bush still holding onto the body.  Especially frustrating is when the ninja or samurai do this as they don't duck when holding a body.  So enemies will walk by and spot them standing upright in a bush with a dead body in their hands..... F8.  God forbid you try to get your character to drag a dead body to a door right after killing that enemy.  50% of the time they'll grab the body, then immediately drop it and start walking or running to the door for no reason.  “No you f.cker, that's not what I f.cking told you to do”  F8.  The number of times my characters did completely random things for no reason is too high to count.

The camera might be the absolute worst part of the game though.  Anything blocked by the camera is essentially unreachable for your characters.  On a narrow pathway with walls around it?  Gotta swing the camera so it's centered on the pathway so you can get your character to go down that path.  Want to go around that corner up ahead?  Well you can't just click around the corner, you've got to re-angle the camera so you can see down that pathway.  Want to get into that door around the next corner, gotta re-angle the camera.

The game has a severe problem dealing with ground/building levels.  If the camera is not exactly positioned correctly, character prompts like jumping, dropping down, throwing bodies off something become impossible to do.  For instance, it looks like there's a secret path you can jump to over there.  Well, the camera is off by 10 degrees, so the prompt for jumping doesn't appear for your character.  So you assume that secret passage isn't in play.  Then 10 minutes later at a slightly different camera angle you happen to pass by that area again and now the jump prompt appears.  Gee, would've been great if that would've shown up 10 minutes ago, would've saved me a lot of trouble.  Especially awful is being on rooftops as you must constantly swing the camera to move around.  One mission has you assassinating some enemy and there's a 3 level building nearby him. The game has a massive heart attack trying to interpret your actions up there.  You will constantly walk places you don't want to walk, jump down when you don't want to jump down, hookshot when you don't want to hookshot, etc.  Especially fun is that the prompt for the hookshot spots are always visible so you'll want to walk somewhere and keep getting the hookshot prompt because where you want to walk happens to have a hookshot prompt in the background somewhere.

The game has some inconsistencies with its noise mechanic.  To give a simple example of this, one of your characters has a technique allowing them to whistle.  Guards and villagers in range will be lured by this.  Sometimes enemies who are clearly highlighted blue indicating they'll hear this noise somehow won't hear it and continue along their way.  Other times enemies who are clearly not highlighted and outside of the range will hear the sound and come investigate.

Another problem with the game is that the vast majority of levels play out almost exactly the same due to the lack of enough puzzle elements.  There are only 4 enemies in the game.  Villagers who won't attack but will run away or report your position.  Guards who can be killed by everyone and be lured/distracted.  StrawHats who can be killed by everyone but won't leave their positions by lures and who will only briefly look at a distraction.  Samurai who work like StrawHats but can only be killed by your Samurai or by shooting them and then running up and stabbing them.  Samurai can also see through Aiko's disguise.  You'll have seen pretty much everything by level 6 but there're 13 levels total.  There's just not enough puzzle here to remain interesting and the vast majority of the puzzle is the same exact thing.  Picking off lone enemies or figuring out which enemy you can lure out and kill in a spot where someone else can't see them dying.

Shadow Tactics has some good ideas but the execution is amateurish.  There simply isn't enough new content/puzzle elements to warrant the number of levels in the game.  The camera, cursor, and random actions your characters take will provide no end of frustrations and swearing.  The game simply isn't polished enough to provide a worthwhile experience.

This game is tedious.  There is exactly ONE solution to every level.  You job is die an extraordinary number of times trying to discover the one, single way that the developers want you to solve the puzzle.  There is absolutely zero room for creativity or spontaneity.  If you step out of the correct path for even a split second, you die.

Ultimately, this game tests your willingness to commit time.  If you are willing to sit through enough deaths to finally stumble upon the only right way to finish a level, then you will get to repeat the whole stupid exercise over again in a new map.  There is really no skill or learning, just grinding through death after death.  

If you dont mind this type of game (i.e. you like Sudoku puzzles), then this game is for you.  But if you like creative, emergent stealth games, then give this one a pass.

Positioning each of the 5 characters is time-consuming, and the fact that you can only give one order to each in the Shadow thing is whack. I can tell them to go kill someone and pick up the body (a single command), but then they just stand there waiting for me to take control and hide it. Simply allowing a chained string of commands would make this game great because it'd be really fun to create elaborate Shadow schemes and then watch them unfold.

Another useful addition would be a 'follow' command. As in, "Hey, we all have to move to the other side of the map to exit the level, so follow me and let's go together! Nope. Gotta do it one by one. [h1]In true samurai style, [i]Shadow Tactics[/i] is a perpetual trial of patience.[/h1]
[i]Shadow Tactics: Blades of the Shogun[/i] is a game I've had my eye on for an incredibly long time at this point, yet I never quite got around to until recently.  I loved the [b]art[/b], I loved the look of the [b]strategic gameplay[/b], I loved the [b]culture[/b], I loved the [b]price[/b], and I really loved that it seemed to always have [b]Overwhelmingly Positive[/b] reviews.  And while I tend to find it blasphemous to leave a review on a game you haven't completed, I'll attempt to be as blunt as possible- [b]I can't fucking bring myself to complete this game.[/b]

This is my first negative review and it breaks my heart to leave one, but I was so [b]immensely disappointed[/b] with [i]Shadow Tactics[/i] that I feel like I ended up with a completely different game than everyone else.  While there are some aforementioned, albeit it occasionally subjective, redeeming qualities of this game, there's one [b]massive negative[/b].  Above all else, [i]Shadow Tactics[/i] is an [b]inconsistent, perpetual trial of patience[/b], fueled by the somewhat controversial design decision to not include a pause button.  While it seems the massive majority of people adore this game, you'll find the massive majority of negative reviews and discussion surrounding this game will revolve around this design choice.

[i]Shadow Tactics[/i] is a [b]really inconsistent[/b] trial and error game, and while it tends to be really satisfying to pull off combos and sweep areas clean without things going disastrously wrong, it never quite feels worth it after an hour of fighting the control scheme, and on not that uncommon of an occasion, it's hard to pinpoint what exactly went [i]right[/i] that one time it worked.  [b]The challenge of [i]Shadow Tactics[/i] never feels like it comes from how you're going to approach a situation, but rather how you're going to get the controls to actually work enough to pull it off[/b]; an issue that's, again, exacerbated by the lack of a pause button.  All of this is further compounded by the really spotty, limited ability to barely queue up actions for multiple characters to execute at the same time.

[i]Shadow Tactics[/i] is a trial of patience above all else, and the control scheme doesn't even attempt to meet you halfway.  After 15 hours of busting my ass to give this game a fair shake, I got exhausted of the constant, cyclical sunk cost loop I found myself in.
